# Dulles International Airport Main Terminal

## History and Design Philosophy

The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal stands as a seminal work of mid-century modern architecture and a pivotal artifact of the jet age , . Its history is inextricably linked to the vision of Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen, whose design fundamentally reimagined the relationship between travelers, aircraft, and the built environment of the airport , . The project began in earnest after Saarinen and his firm, Eero Saarinen and Associates of Hamden, Connecticut, were selected as architects in 1958 under contract with the Civil Aeronautics Administration , . Construction commenced on September 2, 1958, marking the beginning of an ambitious endeavor to create a facility that would not only serve as a functional hub but also embody the dynamism and optimism of air travel , . The airport was conceived as the world's first airport specifically engineered for commercial jet travel, a forward-looking decision that distinguished it from earlier airports designed for propeller-driven aircraft , . Saarinen's approach was revolutionary; he prioritized the passenger experience above all else, designing a space that expressed "the movement and excitement of modern travel by air" and symbolized the connection between the ground and the sky . This philosophy centered on monumentality, elegance, practicality, and a seamless flow of movement, aiming to streamline passenger journey from unloading areas to their aircraft through innovative design , .

The terminal's opening on November 17, 1962, was a momentous occasion, officially inaugurated by President John F. Kennedy , , . The dedication ceremony also included President Dwight D. Eisenhower, underscoring the national significance of the new airport . Saarinen himself described the completed terminal as "the best thing I have ever done," a profound statement of personal and professional achievement that highlights its deep importance in his oeuvre , . However, his untimely death in 1961 meant he never witnessed the completion of his magnum opus . The initial design solved a critical challenge of the era: how to efficiently connect a large passenger terminal to distant aircraft parking stands without imposing long walks on travelers or requiring costly modifications to the planes themselves . Saarinen’s solution was the "mobile lounge"—a vehicle-based system that transported passengers directly from the Main Terminal to the aircraft . This innovation eliminated the need for sprawling concourses or lengthy corridors, representing a highly flexible and human-centric approach to airport design . The Chrysler/Budd-designed mobile lounges, each 54 feet long and capable of carrying up to 102 passengers, became an iconic feature of the airport for four decades . This system was a cornerstone of Saarinen's philosophy, emphasizing technological integration and efficient, human-scale movement within the aviation infrastructure . Despite its eventual replacement for some routes, the enduring legacy of the mobile lounge system remains, with 19 of the original vehicles still in service as of 2025, a testament to both their durability and the airport's respect for its architectural heritage .

The historical significance of the Saarinen-designed terminal is widely acknowledged. It received the prestigious First Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects in 1966, cementing its place in architectural history . Further recognition came in 1988 when it was awarded the AIA Twenty-five Year Award, which honors buildings that have stood the test of time and continue to demonstrate excellence . The building's cultural impact extended beyond the architectural community; in 1982, it was featured on a U.S. Postal Service stamp honoring Eero Saarinen, highlighting its status as a national landmark . This recognition, however, has been shadowed by a persistent conflict between preservationists and aviation regulators. In 1978, the terminal was nominated for inclusion on the National Register of Historic Places, a move championed by those who wished to protect Saarinen's masterpiece from potential alterations or demolition . The nomination process was ultimately unsuccessful due to opposition from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which cited concerns related to the operational needs of a growing airport . This FAA opposition underscores a fundamental tension that has defined the terminal's history: the struggle between preserving a celebrated piece of architectural heritage and adapting a vital transportation asset to meet the escalating demands of modern air travel. This conflict continues to shape the terminal's present and future, making its history not just a chronicle of construction and renovation, but a narrative of competing values and priorities in American infrastructure.

## Physical Structure and Architectural Features

The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal is an exemplary embodiment of mid-century modernist architecture, characterized by its sweeping forms, monumental scale, and innovative engineering , . Designed by Eero Saarinen, the structure was intended to be a dynamic and elegant gateway to the nation's capital, reflecting the optimism and technological advancement of the jet age . The original two-level structure, upon its completion in 1962, measured 600 feet in length and 200 feet in width, with a total floor area of 500,000 square feet , . The total cost for this pioneering design was $108.3 million, a significant investment at the time . The primary materials used were glass, metal, and concrete, chosen to create a light, airy, and futuristic atmosphere . The most iconic and defining feature of the terminal is its vast, concave cable-suspended roof . This roof is supported by 32 slanted reinforced concrete colonnades, arranged in groups of 16 along each facade . These colonnades are not uniform; the northern columns stand 65 feet tall while the southern columns are shorter at 40 feet, a deliberate design choice by Saarinen to emphasize dynamism and direct the eye towards the runways , . Each column was bush-hammered for texture and reinforced with 14 to 20 short tons of Bethlehem Steel rebar, showcasing a blend of aesthetic and structural sophistication . The roof itself rises 65 feet above the main passenger level on the side facing the airfield and 45 feet above the passenger approach, creating a sense of openness and grandeur .

The interior design of the terminal was meticulously planned to facilitate a smooth and intuitive passenger flow, a central tenet of Saarinen's design philosophy . The passenger services are organized on two distinct levels beneath the single, uninterrupted roof plane . The Upper Level is dedicated to ticketing and security screening, serving as the point of embarkation for departing passengers . The Lower Level houses arrivals, baggage claim, and ground transportation facilities, providing a clear separation of incoming and outgoing traffic . This vertical zoning is complemented by a horizontal organization based on the concept of a "central spine" or "white square plaza" hub . From this central core, pedestrian connections radiate outwards to the various concourses, ensuring that all gates remain easily accessible . The design incorporated moving walkways and clear blue signage to guide passengers efficiently through the terminal . Furthermore, the layout was designed to provide passengers with unobstructed views of the active runways from the departures level, reinforcing the theme of flight and adding a dramatic element to the waiting experience . The control tower, another integral part of the original design, stands 177 feet tall and originally housed a glass-enclosed cab, though it was decommissioned in 2007 , . The reflecting pool, another prominent original feature, contributes to the serene and contemplative atmosphere envisioned by Saarinen .

Over the years, the physical footprint of the terminal has expanded significantly, yet the architectural integrity of Saarinen's vision has remained a guiding principle. The most substantial expansion occurred between 1993 and 1996, when the terminal was doubled in length from 600 feet to 1,240 feet , . This project added more than 500,000 square feet of floor space, bringing the total to 1.1 million square feet , . Critically, this expansion was executed with meticulous care to replicate Saarinen's original design language. The new west and east annexes seamlessly continued the curved roofline and incorporated the same glass curtainwall, ensuring a cohesive aesthetic across the entire structure . The expansion was designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM), the same firm responsible for the original construction, further guaranteeing fidelity to the founder's vision . The expanded terminal maintains the same fundamental layout, with two basement levels accommodating essential infrastructure. The first basement level houses the main security checkpoints and the 8,500-square-foot Capital One Lounge, while the second basement contains the 54,500-square-foot AeroTrain station , . The addition of four Z gates along the south facade allowed for direct aircraft loading and unloading, a modern convenience that was integrated into the historic fabric of the building . The terminal's evolution demonstrates a remarkable ability to adapt and grow without compromising the powerful architectural statement first made by Eero Saarinen. As of 2025, the structure continues to operate as the sole passenger terminal for the airport, serving as the central hub for all airlines and connecting passengers to the five satellite concourses .

## Evolution and Major Renovations

From its inception, the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal has undergone a series of transformative renovations and expansions, each aimed at balancing the preservation of Eero Saarinen's architectural vision with the relentless pressure of increasing passenger demand and evolving aviation technology. The terminal's history is a testament to adaptive reuse, where each phase of development has sought to enhance functionality without erasing the character of the original design. The earliest significant intervention occurred between 1978 and 1980, when the architectural firm HOK was engaged to undertake major renovations . While specific details of this project are not fully elaborated in the provided sources, it marked one of the first instances of a concerted effort to modernize the facility shortly after its opening, likely addressing initial operational challenges and preparing the terminal for higher volumes of traffic. This early renovation set a precedent for future projects, establishing a pattern of periodic upgrades to maintain the terminal's relevance and efficiency. The next major chapter in the terminal's evolution was the extensive expansion program completed in 1996. This project, designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM), was a landmark undertaking that doubled the terminal's length from 600 feet to 1,240 feet and increased its floor space from 500,000 to 1.1 million square feet , , . The expansion was not merely a quantitative increase; it was a qualitative one, executed with strict adherence to Saarinen's original design principles. The new wings seamlessly replicated the curved roofline and glass curtainwall, ensuring a unified architectural identity across the entire structure . This careful replication demonstrated a deep institutional commitment to preserving the terminal's historical and aesthetic value, even as it was being expanded to accommodate the needs of a burgeoning airline industry.

The period from 2000 to 2010 represented a significant technological leap for the Main Terminal, driven largely by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA). This era saw the introduction of several critical pieces of infrastructure that reshaped passenger connectivity and security protocols. A key development during this time was the addition of Z Gates, which opened in 2005 . These gates provide direct access to aircraft along the south facade of the terminal, offering a convenient alternative to the traditional mobile lounge system and enhancing the passenger experience . Perhaps the most transformative project of this decade was the construction of the AeroTrain system. To alleviate congestion and improve efficiency for passengers traveling to the midfield concourses, the old mobile lounge system was replaced by an automated people mover . The AeroTrain operates on an underground dual-track system, with stations strategically positioned to minimize walking distances to airline gates . The total cost of the AeroTrain program was $1.4 billion, encompassing the construction of tunnels, stations, and the train vehicles themselves . The system officially opened to passengers on January 26, 2010, featuring 29 vehicles that travel at a maximum speed of 42 miles per hour, with an average wait time of approximately two minutes during peak periods , . The AeroTrain platform, located approximately 60 feet below ground, is a marvel of engineering in its own right, spanning the full length of the Main Terminal and comprising four distinct levels, including a massive 54,500-square-foot AeroTrain Platform . This project marked a decisive shift in the terminal's operational paradigm, replacing Saarinen's vehicle-based system with a fixed-guideway transit solution for the majority of concourse connections .

Further refinements to the terminal's layout and security infrastructure continued throughout the 2000s and into the 2020s. A significant change was the relocation of the primary security checkpoint from the ticketing level to the first basement level . This move, which involved the construction of a 121,700-square-foot Security Mezzanine, was designed to alleviate congestion and streamline the flow of arriving and departing passengers , . The new security checkpoint opened in September 2009, followed by the AeroTrain station in the second basement, which opened in early 2010 . This vertical reorganization of functions represents a departure from Saarinen's original two-level concept, prioritizing security and operational efficiency in response to post-9/11 realities. More recently, the terminal has seen upgrades focused on customs and baggage handling systems. The MWAA issued a Request for Information (RFI) in August 2023 seeking RFID-based tracking solutions for secure document containers used in the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Modified Egress program within the Main Terminal's International Arrivals Building . This initiative reflects an ongoing effort to integrate modern technology to improve the efficiency and security of international arrivals processing . Additionally, pre-solicitation terms were approved in May 2024 for planning and design services related to the reconstruction of Runway 1R-19L and associated taxiways, indicating that the terminal's infrastructure continues to evolve in coordination with the airfield . Even the historic mobile lounges have seen maintenance-focused improvements, as evidenced by a solicitation for new wheel hubs issued in December 2025 . This ongoing cycle of renovation, from major expansions to targeted upgrades, illustrates the terminal's continuous adaptation to the changing landscape of aviation, navigating the complex interplay between its revered architectural past and the pragmatic demands of its present-day operations.

## Operational Infrastructure and Passenger Experience

The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal serves as the central nexus for all passenger activity at the airport, functioning as the sole passenger terminal and a sophisticated hub connecting to five distinct concourses: A, B, C, D, and Z . The passenger experience is shaped by a multi-layered operational infrastructure designed to manage the flow of millions of travelers annually while offering a range of services, amenities, and points of connection. Upon arrival at the terminal, passengers enter the Lower Level, which is dedicated to arrivals, baggage claim, and ground transportation . This level houses the International Arrivals Building, which includes Baggage Claim carousels 1–15 and is the designated location for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) inspections for all incoming international flights , . After clearing CBP, passengers must collect all their luggage before exiting the secure facility, as re-entry is not permitted . For connecting international passengers, the process involves re-checking luggage and undergoing TSA screening again . The Lower Level also provides access to the Silver Line Express bus, which connects to the Metro station, and the AeroTrain platform for Midfield Concourses A, B, and C . Pre-security amenities on this level include the District Chophouse restaurant, Cafe Americana food court, and the USO Lounge, which offers services to military personnel and their families , , .

Departing passengers navigate the Upper Level, which is dedicated to ticketing and security screening . As of June 2025, this level is served by three TSA Security Checkpoints: a West checkpoint, an East checkpoint, and a separate TSA PreCheck lane . Once cleared through security, passengers enter the expansive post-security area, which serves as the common space for all concourses. This area is equipped with free Wi-Fi ('FlyDulles' network), numerous charging stations, and public art installations to enhance the waiting experience . The main post-security facilities include the Capital One Lounge, a spacious 8,500-square-foot venue offering a full buffet, bar service, and relaxation rooms , , . Post-security dining options are abundant, with establishments like Ben's Chili Bowl, Rappahannock Oyster Bar, and &pizza located in Concourse B, among others . The terminal also provides family-friendly services, including nursing rooms, and specialized shops catering to children's needs, such as Capitol City Ink and InMotion, which offer toys, electronics, and healthy snacks , . CLEAR enrollment kiosks are available on the Departures Level for expedited background checks, and members can use them to bypass standard lines and enter TSA PreCheck lanes directly .

Connecting passengers to the five satellite concourses is a critical function managed by a hybrid system of automated transit and shuttle services. The primary mode of post-security transport is the AeroTrain, an automated people mover that travels on an underground track to Concourses A, B, and C , . The AeroTrain system, which opened in 2010, offers rapid transit times, with a journey between stations taking approximately 72 seconds . Transfer times between concourses are kept to a minimum, typically ranging from 3 to 7 minutes, a design feature intended to reduce traveler stress and optimize queuing for boarding . For example, a transfer from Concourse B to Concourse C takes 3-5 minutes, while an arrival from Terminal A to Concourse B via AeroTrain takes 4-6 minutes . In addition to the AeroTrain, direct pedestrian bridges connect the Main Terminal to Concourses A, B, and Z, allowing for quick and easy transfers , . The final concourse, D, is serviced by a shuttle bus system using the historic Mobile Lounges , . This combination of high-speed automated transit and reliable shuttle buses ensures that all gates remain well-connected to the central hub. Accessibility is a key consideration throughout the terminal, with designated accessible parking spaces available in all public lots and garages, wheelchair-accessible shuttle buses provided free of charge, and assistance available for passengers with disabilities in compliance with the Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) , .

## Ground Transportation and Regional Connectivity

The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal is strategically situated 26 miles from downtown Washington, D.C., in suburban Virginia, necessitating robust and diverse ground transportation infrastructure to connect passengers to the metropolitan region . Since its opening in 1962, the foundational link to the surrounding highway network has been the Dulles Access Highway, which was constructed concurrently with the terminal to ensure immediate vehicular access . This highway provides a direct route for private vehicles, taxis, and rideshare services, forming the backbone of the airport's surface transportation system. Over the decades, the reliance on road-based transit has been supplemented by increasingly sophisticated public transit options, culminating in a direct rail connection that dramatically enhances regional accessibility. The most significant development in this regard was the extension of the Washington Metro's Silver Line, which finally reached the airport on November 15, 2022, after over six decades of planning and phased construction involving multiple government agencies , . This 23.1-mile extension added 11 new stations, a rail-car storage yard, and a maintenance facility, providing a fast, reliable, and environmentally friendly alternative to driving . The Silver Line Phase 2 connects the Main Terminal to downtown Washington, D.C., with each ride taking approximately one hour and costing around $6.75 .

The integration of the Metro Silver Line into the airport's infrastructure required the construction of an indoor pedestrian tunnel equipped with moving sidewalks . This tunnel links the Main Terminal Building directly to the new Dulles Airport Station, eliminating exposure to weather and providing a seamless transition for passengers arriving by rail . The tunnel also connects to Parking Garage 1, facilitating easy access for those combining a drive with a train ride . The establishment of this direct rail link marks a transformative moment for the airport, fundamentally altering the dynamics of regional mobility and reducing the environmental impact associated with airport-related traffic . In addition to the Metro, the airport is served by Washington Flyer taxi cabs, which exclusively service Dulles, and fares into Washington, D.C. typically range from $60 to $70, making it a more expensive but direct option for travelers . Ride-sharing services are also widely available at designated pickup zones outside the terminal. The airport's parking facilities are comprehensive, offering a range of options to suit different budgets and travel durations. Public parking is available in Terminal Lot, Garage 1, Garage 2, and Economy Parking, with all facilities providing free shuttle bus service to and from the Main Terminal entrance . All Dulles airport parking shuttle buses are wheelchair accessible, ensuring that the ground transportation network is inclusive for all passengers .

For individuals with disabilities, the airport provides a suite of services designed to ensure a barrier-free travel experience. Accessible parking spaces are designated throughout all public parking facilities, clearly marked and requiring a valid government-issued disabled plate or placard . When parking facilities are full, uniformed parking assistants are available to assist patrons in locating a space and verifying credentials on-site . The shuttle buses that serve all parking areas are equipped to accommodate wheelchairs, and patrons can call 703-572-4500 to request assistance with finding a spot . Beyond physical access, the airport complies with the Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA), which mandates that airlines provide timely assistance to passengers with disabilities . This assistance covers the entire journey, from curbside drop-off to the gate, and includes help with navigating security checkpoints, accessing restrooms, and transferring between aircraft . Airlines may request a credible verbal assurance of the nature of the requested assistance but are prohibited from inquiring about the specific disability itself . These policies and services reflect a comprehensive approach to mobility, integrating advanced public transit with a wide array of ground transportation options and accessibility support to meet the diverse needs of the millions of travelers who pass through the Main Terminal each year.

## Strategic Future and Contemporary Developments

As of late 2025, the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal finds itself at a historic crossroads, caught between its celebrated architectural legacy and a bold, and controversial, strategic vision for the future. The contemporary developments are defined by a stark dichotomy: on one hand, there are plans for aggressive expansion projected to triple the airport's passenger capacity; on the other, there is a formal federal initiative calling for the complete replacement of the iconic Saarinen-designed terminal. This situation has created an existential crisis for the terminal, forcing a reckoning with its role as both a cherished national monument and a functional transportation hub. The foundation for this new direction was laid with the approval of the Washington Dulles International Airport Master Plan on July 16, 2025 . This official FAA-compliant document supersedes the previous master plan from 1985 and outlines a path to handle up to 90 million annual passengers , . The plan projects a phased growth strategy, with targets of 38 million passengers by 2030, 45 million by 2045, and the ultimate goal of 90 million, supported by a corresponding increase in infrastructure, including the construction of 218 gates . A key component of this expansion is the construction of a new midfield concourse, which is already under construction and expected to open in the fall of 2026 . The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA) has already moved forward with this vision, selecting the architectural firm HOK in July 2025 to design a major expansion that will add more than 2.8 million square feet of new space .

This expansion plan, however, appears to contain a fundamental contradiction. While the MWAA is pursuing a new construction program, the stated goal of this program is to honor Eero Saarinen's 1960s architecture . HOK's design team, led by co-CEO Susan Klumpp Williams, emphasizes a deep respect for Saarinen's work, describing it as representing the "golden age of aviation" . This suggests a strategy of expanding and augmenting the existing terminal rather than replacing it entirely. This nuanced approach seems to directly conflict with a much more radical proposal announced in December 2025. On December 2, President Donald Trump publicly criticized the existing airport, calling it "not a good airport" despite acknowledging "a great building" . He then stated his intent to "rebuild Dulles airport." This sentiment was formalized on December 5, 2025, when the U.S. Department of Transportation launched a revitalization initiative inviting proposals to "construct completely new terminals and concourses" to replace or build upon the existing Saarinen-designed structures . This federal directive represents a seismic shift in policy, signaling a potential end for the original terminal after more than six decades of service. The discrepancy between the MWAA's preservation-oriented expansion plan and the federal government's demolition-oriented master plan creates a state of profound uncertainty regarding the terminal's ultimate fate.

In the midst of this strategic turmoil, the airport continues to undergo a flurry of ongoing upgrade initiatives, suggesting that the terminal is still being actively improved even as its long-term viability is debated. In October 2025, the MWAA issued a solicitation for Construction Manager at Risk (CMR) services for a comprehensive program covering baggage improvements, terminal and concourse rehabilitation, and terminal lobby and baggage reconfiguration . Simultaneously, another solicitation was issued for contracts related to the reconstruction of Runway 1R-19L and associated taxiways, indicating that the airfield infrastructure is also being upgraded in tandem with the terminal . Furthermore, the airport is investing in modernizing its international arrival processes, as shown by the RFI for RFID-based tracking systems for CBP operations in the Main Terminal's International Arrivals Building . These active procurement efforts create a confusing picture: is the airport investing in the future of the old terminal, or is it laying the groundwork for a new one? The Dulles Main Terminal's future is now defined by this central conflict. The resolution of this internal contradiction—whether the MWAA will align with the federal push for demolition or continue down the path of Saarinen-inspired expansion—will determine whether the iconic structure survives as a preserved monument or becomes the site for a new generation of aviation infrastructure. This pivotal moment in its history will define the legacy of the "best thing I have ever done" for generations to come.

Designed by Eero Saarinen, the structure was intended to be a dynamic and elegant gateway to the nation's capital, reflecting the optimism and technological advancement of the jet age.
The original two-level structure, upon its completion in 1962, measured 600 feet in length and 200 feet in width, with a total floor area of 500,000 square feet.
The total cost for this pioneering design was $108.3 million, a significant investment at the time.
The primary materials used for the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal were glass, metal, and concrete, chosen to create a light, airy, and futuristic atmosphere.
The most iconic and defining feature of the terminal is its vast, concave cable-suspended roof.
This roof is supported by 32 slanted reinforced concrete colonnades, arranged in groups of 16 along each facade.

These colonnades are not uniform; the northern columns stand 65 feet tall while the southern columns are shorter at 40 feet, a deliberate design choice by Saarinen to emphasize dynamism and direct the eye towards the runways.
Each column was bush-hammered for texture and reinforced with 14 to 20 short tons of Bethlehem Steel rebar, showcasing a blend of aesthetic and structural sophistication.
The roof itself rises 65 feet above the main passenger level on the side facing the airfield and 45 feet above the passenger approach, creating a sense of openness and grandeur.
The interior design of the terminal was meticulously planned to facilitate a smooth and intuitive passenger flow, a central tenet of Saarinen's design philosophy.
The passenger services are organized on two distinct levels beneath the single, uninterrupted roof plane.
The Upper Level is dedicated to ticketing and security screening, serving as the point of embarkation for departing passengers.
The Lower Level houses arrivals, baggage claim, and ground transportation facilities, providing a clear separation of incoming and outgoing traffic.
This vertical zoning is complemented by a horizontal organization based on the concept of a "central spine" or "white square plaza" hub.
From this central core, pedestrian connections radiate outwards to the various concourses, ensuring that all gates remain easily accessible.
The design incorporated moving walkways and clear blue signage to guide passengers efficiently through the terminal.

Furthermore, the layout was designed to provide passengers with unobstructed views of the active runways from the departures level, reinforcing the theme of flight and adding a dramatic element to the waiting experience.
The control tower, another integral part of the original design, stands 177 feet tall and originally housed a glass-enclosed cab, though it was decommissioned in 2007.
The reflecting pool, another prominent original feature, contributes to the serene and contemplative atmosphere envisioned by Saarinen.
Over the years, the physical footprint of the terminal has expanded significantly, yet the architectural integrity of Saarinen's vision has remained a guiding principle.
The most substantial expansion occurred between 1993 and 1996, when the terminal was doubled in length from 600 feet to 1,240 feet.
This project added more than 500,000 square feet of floor space, bringing the total to 1.1 million square feet.
Critically, this expansion was executed with meticulous care to replicate Saarinen's original design language.
The new west and east annexes seamlessly continued the curved roofline and incorporated the same glass curtainwall, ensuring a cohesive aesthetic across the entire structure.
The expansion was designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM), the same firm responsible for the original construction, further guaranteeing fidelity to the founder's vision.
The expanded terminal maintains the same fundamental layout, with two basement levels accommodating essential infrastructure.
The first basement level houses the main security checkpoints and the 8,500-square-foot Capital One Lounge, while the second basement contains the 54,500-square-foot AeroTrain station.
The addition of four Z gates along the south facade allowed for direct aircraft loading and unloading, a modern convenience that was integrated into the historic fabric of the building.
The terminal's evolution demonstrates a remarkable ability to adapt and grow without compromising the powerful architectural statement first made by Eero Saarinen.
As of 2025, the structure continues to operate as the sole passenger terminal for the airport, serving as the central hub for all airlines and connecting passengers to the five satellite concourses.
Eero Saarinen and Associates are the architects of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal.
The original opening date of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal was November 17, 1962.
The original dimensions of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal were 600 ft (length) × 200 ft (width).
The original floor area of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal was 500,000 sq ft.
The total original cost of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal was $108.3 million.
The final dimensions of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal (Post-1996 Expansion) are 1,240 ft (length) × 150 ft (width).
The final floor area of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal (Post-1996 Expansion) is 1.1 million sq ft.
The primary materials used for the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal are Glass, metal, and concrete.
The roof system of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal is a concave cable-suspended roof supported by 32 slanted concrete colonnades.
The column heights of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal are 65 ft on the North facade and 40 ft on the South facade.
The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal has two basement levels for security, the AeroTrain station, and lounges.
The control tower height of the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal is 177 ft, and it was decommissioned in 2007.
There are 32 slanted concrete colonnades in the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal, with 16 per facade.

From its inception, the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal has undergone a series of transformative renovations and expansions, each aimed at balancing the preservation of Eero Saarinen's architectural vision with the relentless pressure of increasing passenger demand and evolving aviation technology.
The terminal's history is a testament to adaptive reuse, where each phase of development has sought to enhance functionality without erasing the character of the original design.
The earliest significant intervention occurred between 1978 and 1980, when the architectural firm HOK was engaged to undertake major renovations.
This early renovation set a precedent for future projects, establishing a pattern of periodic upgrades to maintain the terminal's relevance and efficiency.
The next major chapter in the terminal's evolution was the extensive expansion program completed in 1996.

This project, designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM), was a landmark undertaking that doubled the terminal's length from 600 feet to 1,240 feet and increased its floor space from 500,000 to 1.1 million square feet.
The expansion was not merely a quantitative increase; it was a qualitative one, executed with strict adherence to Saarinen's original design principles.
The new wings seamlessly replicated the curved roofline and glass curtainwall, ensuring a unified architectural identity across the entire structure.

This careful replication demonstrated a deep institutional commitment to preserving the terminal's historical and aesthetic value, even as it was being expanded to accommodate the needs of a burgeoning airline industry.
The period from 2000 to 2010 represented a significant technological leap for the Main Terminal, driven largely by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA).
This era saw the introduction of several critical pieces of infrastructure that reshaped passenger connectivity and security protocols.
A key development during this time was the addition of Z Gates, which opened in 2005.

These Z Gates provide direct access to aircraft along the south facade of the terminal, offering a convenient alternative to the traditional mobile lounge system and enhancing the passenger experience.
Perhaps the most transformative project of this decade was the construction of the AeroTrain system.
To alleviate congestion and improve efficiency for passengers traveling to the midfield concourses, the old mobile lounge system was replaced by an automated people mover.
The AeroTrain operates on an underground dual-track system, with stations strategically positioned to minimize walking distances to airline gates.
The total cost of the AeroTrain program was $1.4 billion, encompassing the construction of tunnels, stations, and the train vehicles themselves.

The AeroTrain system officially opened to passengers on January 26, 2010, featuring 29 vehicles that travel at a maximum speed of 42 miles per hour, with an average wait time of approximately two minutes during peak periods.

The AeroTrain platform, located approximately 60 feet below ground, is a marvel of engineering in its own right, spanning the full length of the Main Terminal and comprising four distinct levels, including a massive 54,500-square-foot AeroTrain Platform.

This project marked a decisive shift in the terminal's operational paradigm, replacing Saarinen's vehicle-based system with a fixed-guideway transit solution for the majority of concourse connections.
Further refinements to the terminal's layout and security infrastructure continued throughout the 2000s and into the 2020s.
A significant change was the relocation of the primary security checkpoint from the ticketing level to the first basement level.
This move, which involved the construction of a 121,700-square-foot Security Mezzanine, was designed to alleviate congestion and streamline the flow of arriving and departing passengers.
The new security checkpoint opened in September 2009, followed by the AeroTrain station in the second basement, which opened in early 2010.
This vertical reorganization of functions represents a departure from Saarinen's original two-level concept, prioritizing security and operational efficiency in response to post-9/11 realities.
More recently, the terminal has seen upgrades focused on customs and baggage handling systems.

The MWAA issued a Request for Information (RFI) in August 2023 seeking RFID-based tracking solutions for secure document containers used in the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Modified Egress program within the Main Terminal's International Arrivals Building.
This initiative reflects an ongoing effort to integrate modern technology to improve the efficiency and security of international arrivals processing.

Additionally, pre-solicitation terms were approved in May 2024 for planning and design services related to the reconstruction of Runway 1R-19L and associated taxiways, indicating that the terminal's infrastructure continues to evolve in coordination with the airfield.
Even the historic mobile lounges have seen maintenance-focused improvements, as evidenced by a solicitation for new wheel hubs issued in December 2025.

This ongoing cycle of renovation, from major expansions to targeted upgrades, illustrates the terminal's continuous adaptation to the changing landscape of aviation, navigating the complex interplay between its revered architectural past and the pragmatic demands of its present-day operations.

The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal serves as the central nexus for all passenger activity at the airport, functioning as the sole passenger terminal and a sophisticated hub connecting to five distinct concourses: A, B, C, D, and Z.

The passenger experience is shaped by a multi-layered operational infrastructure designed to manage the flow of millions of travelers annually while offering a range of services, amenities, and points of connection.
Upon arrival at the terminal, passengers enter the Lower Level, which is dedicated to arrivals, baggage claim, and ground transportation.

This level houses the International Arrivals Building, which includes Baggage Claim carousels 1–15 and is the designated location for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) inspections for all incoming international flights.
After clearing CBP, passengers must collect all their luggage before exiting the secure facility, as re-entry is not permitted.
For connecting international passengers, the process involves re-checking luggage and undergoing TSA screening again.
The Lower Level also provides access to the Silver Line Express bus, which connects to the Metro station, and the AeroTrain platform for Midfield Concourses A, B, and C.
Pre-security amenities on this level include the District Chophouse restaurant, Cafe Americana food court, and the USO Lounge, which offers services to military personnel and their families.
Departing passengers navigate the Upper Level, which is dedicated to ticketing and security screening.
As of June 2025, this level is served by three TSA Security Checkpoints: a West checkpoint, an East checkpoint, and a separate TSA PreCheck lane.
Once cleared through security, passengers enter the expansive post-security area, which serves as the common space for all concourses.
This area is equipped with free Wi-Fi ('FlyDulles' network), numerous charging stations, and public art installations to enhance the waiting experience.
The main post-security facilities include the Capital One Lounge, a spacious 8,500-square-foot venue offering a full buffet, bar service, and relaxation rooms.
Post-security dining options are abundant, with establishments like Ben's Chili Bowl, Rappahannock Oyster Bar, and &pizza located in Concourse B, among others.

The terminal also provides family-friendly services, including nursing rooms, and specialized shops catering to children's needs, such as Capitol City Ink and InMotion, which offer toys, electronics, and healthy snacks.
CLEAR enrollment kiosks are available on the Departures Level for expedited background checks, and members can use them to bypass standard lines and enter TSA PreCheck lanes directly.
Connecting passengers to the five satellite concourses is a critical function managed by a hybrid system of automated transit and shuttle services.
The primary mode of post-security transport is the AeroTrain, an automated people mover that travels on an underground track to Concourses A, B, and C.
The AeroTrain system, which opened in 2010, offers rapid transit times, with a journey between stations taking approximately 72 seconds.
Transfer times between concourses are kept to a minimum, typically ranging from 3 to 7 minutes, a design feature intended to reduce traveler stress and optimize queuing for boarding.
For example, a transfer from Concourse B to Concourse C takes 3-5 minutes, while an arrival from Terminal A to Concourse B via AeroTrain takes 4-6 minutes.
In addition to the AeroTrain, direct pedestrian bridges connect the Main Terminal to Concourses A, B, and Z, allowing for quick and easy transfers.
The final concourse, D, is serviced by a shuttle bus system using the historic Mobile Lounges.
This combination of high-speed automated transit and reliable shuttle buses ensures that all gates remain well-connected to the central hub.

Accessibility is a key consideration throughout the terminal, with designated accessible parking spaces available in all public lots and garages, wheelchair-accessible shuttle buses provided free of charge, and assistance available for passengers with disabilities in compliance with the Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA).
The AeroTrain is an Automated People Mover that connects to Concourses A, B, and C.
The AeroTrain is an underground dual-track system with a 72-second travel time between stations and opened on January 26, 2010.
Pedestrian Walkways are Walking Paths that provide direct, overhead paths connecting the Main Terminal to Concourses A, B, and Z.
The Mobile Lounge Shuttle uses the historic fleet of 19 Saarinen-era mobile lounges for transport to Concourse D.
Direct Aircraft Access via Pedestrian Bridge allows passengers to exit directly onto the apron to board aircraft at designated Z Gates (Z6-Z10).

The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal is strategically situated 26 miles from downtown Washington, D.C., in suburban Virginia, necessitating robust and diverse ground transportation infrastructure to connect passengers to the metropolitan region.

Since its opening in 1962, the foundational link to the surrounding highway network has been the Dulles Access Highway, which was constructed concurrently with the terminal to ensure immediate vehicular access.
This highway provides a direct route for private vehicles, taxis, and rideshare services, forming the backbone of the airport's surface transportation system.

Over the decades, the reliance on road-based transit has been supplemented by increasingly sophisticated public transit options, culminating in a direct rail connection that dramatically enhances regional accessibility.

The most significant development in this regard was the extension of the Washington Metro's Silver Line, which finally reached the airport on November 15, 2022, after over six decades of planning and phased construction involving multiple government agencies.
This 23.1-mile extension added 11 new stations, a rail-car storage yard, and a maintenance facility, providing a fast, reliable, and environmentally friendly alternative to driving.
The Silver Line Phase 2 connects the Main Terminal to downtown Washington, D.C., with each ride taking approximately one hour and costing around $6.75.
The integration of the Metro Silver Line into the airport's infrastructure required the construction of an indoor pedestrian tunnel equipped with moving sidewalks.
This tunnel links the Main Terminal Building directly to the new Dulles Airport Station, eliminating exposure to weather and providing a seamless transition for passengers arriving by rail.
The tunnel also connects to Parking Garage 1, facilitating easy access for those combining a drive with a train ride.

The establishment of this direct rail link marks a transformative moment for the airport, fundamentally altering the dynamics of regional mobility and reducing the environmental impact associated with airport-related traffic.

In addition to the Metro, the airport is served by Washington Flyer taxi cabs, which exclusively service Dulles, and fares into Washington, D.C. typically range from $60 to $70, making it a more expensive but direct option for travelers.
Ride-sharing services are also widely available at designated pickup zones outside the terminal.
The airport's parking facilities are comprehensive, offering a range of options to suit different budgets and travel durations.
Public parking is available in Terminal Lot, Garage 1, Garage 2, and Economy Parking, with all facilities providing free shuttle bus service to and from the Main Terminal entrance.
All Dulles airport parking shuttle buses are wheelchair accessible, ensuring that the ground transportation network is inclusive for all passengers.
For individuals with disabilities, the airport provides a suite of services designed to ensure a barrier-free travel experience.
Accessible parking spaces are designated throughout all public parking facilities, clearly marked and requiring a valid government-issued disabled plate or placard.
When parking facilities are full, uniformed parking assistants are available to assist patrons in locating a space and verifying credentials on-site.
The shuttle buses that serve all parking areas are equipped to accommodate wheelchairs, and patrons can call 703-572-4500 to request assistance with finding a spot.
Beyond physical access, the airport complies with the Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA), which mandates that airlines provide timely assistance to passengers with disabilities.
This assistance covers the entire journey, from curbside drop-off to the gate, and includes help with navigating security checkpoints, accessing restrooms, and transferring between aircraft.
Airlines may request a credible verbal assurance of the nature of the requested assistance but are prohibited from inquiring about the specific disability itself.

These policies and services reflect a comprehensive approach to mobility, integrating advanced public transit with a wide array of ground transportation options and accessibility support to meet the diverse needs of the millions of travelers who pass through the Main Terminal each year.
The Dulles Access Highway is a Major arterial road connecting the airport to the regional highway network.
The Dulles Access Highway opened in 1962 alongside the terminal and serves private vehicles, taxis, and rideshares.
The Metrorail Silver Line is a Rapid transit line connecting Dulles to Washington, D.C.
The Metrorail Silver Line was extended to the airport and opened on November 15, 2022, with an indoor tunnel connecting the terminal to the station.
Washington Flyer taxis exclusively serve the airport, and rideshare services are also available.
Airport Shuttles are free bus services connecting parking facilities to the Main Terminal.
Airport Shuttles are operated by the airport for all public parking lots and garages, and all shuttles are wheelchair accessible.
Accessible Parking consists of specialized parking spaces for persons with disabilities.
Accessible Parking is available in all public lots/garages and requires a valid state-issued disabled plate/placard.
The Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) is a federal law mandating assistance for passengers with disabilities.
The Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) requires airlines to provide assistance with navigation, security, and boarding.

As of late 2025, the Dulles International Airport Main Terminal finds itself at a historic crossroads, caught between its celebrated architectural legacy and a bold, and controversial, strategic vision for the future.

The contemporary developments are defined by a stark dichotomy: on one hand, there are plans for aggressive expansion projected to triple the airport's passenger capacity; on the other, there is a formal federal initiative calling for the complete replacement of the iconic Saarinen-designed terminal.
This situation has created an existential crisis for the terminal, forcing a reckoning with its role as both a cherished national monument and a functional transportation hub.
The foundation for this new direction was laid with the approval of the Washington Dulles International Airport Master Plan on July 16, 2025.
This official FAA-compliant document supersedes the previous master plan from 1985 and outlines a path to handle up to 90 million annual passengers.

The plan projects a phased growth strategy, with targets of 38 million passengers by 2030, 45 million by 2045, and the ultimate goal of 90 million, supported by a corresponding increase in infrastructure, including the construction of 218 gates.
A key component of this expansion is the construction of a new midfield concourse, which is already under construction and expected to open in the fall of 2026.

The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA) has already moved forward with this vision, selecting the architectural firm HOK in July 2025 to design a major expansion that will add more than 2.8 million square feet of new space.
This expansion plan, however, appears to contain a fundamental contradiction.
While the MWAA is pursuing a new construction program, the stated goal of this program is to honor Eero Saarinen's 1960s architecture.
HOK's design team, led by co-CEO Susan Klumpp Williams, emphasizes a deep respect for Saarinen's work, describing it as representing the "golden age of aviation."
This suggests a strategy of expanding and augmenting the existing terminal rather than replacing it entirely.
This nuanced approach seems to directly conflict with a much more radical proposal announced in December 2025.
On December 2, President Donald Trump publicly criticized the existing airport, calling it "not a good airport" despite acknowledging "a great building."
He then stated his intent to "rebuild Dulles airport."

This sentiment was formalized on December 5, 2025, when the U.S. Department of Transportation launched a revitalization initiative inviting proposals to "construct completely new terminals and concourses" to replace or build upon the existing Saarinen-designed structures.
This federal directive represents a seismic shift in policy, signaling a potential end for the original terminal after more than six decades of service.

The discrepancy between the MWAA's preservation-oriented expansion plan and the federal government's demolition-oriented master plan creates a state of profound uncertainty regarding the terminal's ultimate fate.

In the midst of this strategic turmoil, the airport continues to undergo a flurry of ongoing upgrade initiatives, suggesting that the terminal is still being actively improved even as its long-term viability is debated.

In October 2025, the MWAA issued a solicitation for Construction Manager at Risk (CMR) services for a comprehensive program covering baggage improvements, terminal and concourse rehabilitation, and terminal lobby and baggage reconfiguration.

Simultaneously, another solicitation was issued for contracts related to the reconstruction of Runway 1R-19L and associated taxiways, indicating that the airfield infrastructure is also being upgraded in tandem with the terminal.

Furthermore, the airport is investing in modernizing its international arrival processes, as shown by the RFI for RFID-based tracking systems for CBP operations in the Main Terminal's International Arrivals Building.
These active procurement efforts create a confusing picture: is the airport investing in the future of the old terminal, or is it laying the groundwork for a new one?
The Dulles Main Terminal's future is now defined by this central conflict.

The resolution of this internal contradiction—whether the MWAA will align with the federal push for demolition or continue down the path of Saarinen-inspired expansion—will determine whether the iconic structure survives as a preserved monument or becomes the site for a new generation of aviation infrastructure.
This pivotal moment in its history will define the legacy of the "best thing I have ever done" for generations to come.

Key takeaways
-------------

*   Opened in 1962, Dulles is the first US airport designed for commercial jets and is the largest in the DC-Maryland-Virginia area, spanning 20 square miles and 11,184 acres.
*   Designed by architect Eero Saarinen, it serves as the main international hub for the DC area. The airport underwent significant expansions from 2000–2011, with additional growth in 2023 to handle 55 million passengers annually.
*   The airport offers multiple travel conveniences like the 24-hour Aerotrain, TSA PreCheck, Global Entry, and various transport options including metro, buses, and taxis. Security wait times average 10–28 minutes.
*   Dulles features free Wifi, charging stations, a wide range of dining options, lounges, shopping, and even a Sleepbox Lounge for rest. Visitors can enjoy local Virginia wines, duty-free shopping, and public art installations.
*   With Going membership plans, you can get real-time alerts from most US airport—including Dulles (IAD)—as soon as prices drop for domestic and international flights. That way, you know you're getting the some of the cheapest flights every time.

Built in 1962, Dulles was the first US airport designed specifically to accommodate commercial jets. At 20 square miles and 11,184 acres, it’s the largest of the three major airports in the DC-Maryland-Virginia (DMV) area; the other two are Baltimore/Washington (BWI) and Reagan National (DCA).

About Dulles International Airport
----------------------------------

Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) was designed by acclaimed Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen and named for John Foster Dulles, Secretary of State from 1953-1959 under President Eisenhower. It serves 32 airlines with four runways (and in the future, a fifth) and is considered the main international hub for the greater DC area.

From 2000 to 2011, the multi-billion dollar [Dulles Development Program (D2)](https://www.mwaa.com/business/dulles-international-airport-capital-improvements) expanded the airport with construction projects like two new parking garages, a fourth runway, a new concourse (Z), a new Air Traffic Control tower, pedestrian walkways and the Aerotrain. Now underway through the end of 2023, the airport’s sustainability-focused Master Plan program is assessing how to further grow and develop the airport; at full build-out, Dulles will handle 55 million passengers a year (150,000 a day).

*   **Airport code:** IAD
*   **Official address:** 1 Saarinen Circle, Dulles, Virginia 20166 
*   **Distance from IAD to Washington, DC:** 26 miles
*   **Transport options:** Metro / Various Buses / Taxi / Rideshare Apps
*   **Airlines served:** 32
*   **Hubs for**: United, Southern Airways Express
*   **Domestic nonstop flights to:** 81 cities
*   **International nonstop flights to:** 52 countries
*   **IAD Terminals:** 1
*   **Concourses:** 5
*   **Gates:** 139
*   **On time departures:** 82%
*   **On time arrivals:** 78%
*   **Security wait times:** 10.5 minutes (on average)
*   **Hours:** 24 hours a day
*   **Official site**: [flydulles.com](https://www.flydulles.com/)‍
*   **Wikipedia:** [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles\_International\_Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport)‍
*   **Approximate # of yearly passengers:** 15,000,000 (2021) 
*   **Approximate # of yearly flights:** 200,000 (2021)

### Airlines Flying From IAD

**Main Terminal:** Aer Lingus—Aeroflot Russian Airlines—Air Canada—Air China Airlines—Air France—Air India—Alaska Airlines—American Airlines—ANA Airlines—Austrian Airlines—Avianca Airlines—British Airways—Brussels Airlines—Cathay Pacific—COPA Airlines—Delta Airlines—Emirates—Ethiopian Airlines—Etihad Airlines—Icelandair—KLM Airlines—Korean Air Lines—Lufthansa—Porter Airlines—Qatar Airways—Royal Air Maroc Airlines—SAS Scandinavian Airlines—Saudia Airlines—South African Airways—Southern Airways Express—Southwest Airlines—Turkish Airlines—United Airlines—Virgin America Airlines—Virgin Atlantic

**Concourse A:** Alitalia—Egyptair—TAP Air Portugal—Volaris Airlines

_Avoid paying more than you should—discover_ [_the best time to book a cheap flight_](https://www.going.com/guides/the-best-time-to-book-a-cheap-flight) _and travel smarter._

### Terminal Layout

**Main Terminal:** Capped by an iconic curved roof, the Terminal is divided into two levels: Upper (Ticketing and Security) and Lower (Arrivals/Baggage Claim and Ground Transportation/Parking).

On the Lower Level at Arrivals/Baggage Claim is the Aerotrain platform (providing access to the A, B, C and Z gates) and as well as the shuttle bus to D gates.

To the right of the Aerotrain platform is the International Arrivals Building, where services and amenities include ATMs, Baggage Claim carousels 1-15, electronic charging stations, the lost property desk, the USO lounge, and at Door 4, access to the Silver Line Express bus. There’s a waiting area immediately outside the International Arrivals Building near Baggage Claim 15; after clearing US Customs, international arrivals come through doors between Baggage Claim 4 and 12.

On the Upper Level, there are four ticketing areas plus two security checkpoint areas, East and West. After clearing security, you can proceed left to the Z gates (Z6-Z10), right to the Mobile Lounge shuttle to Concourses D and C, or proceed straight to the pedestrian walkway to Concourses A and B.

**Concourse A:** Gates A1-A32. Amenities here include the Washington Dulles International Airport Chapel across from gate A32, which welcomes all faiths. Also near Gate 32 is a pet relief area, adjacent to the Virgin Atlantic lounge. The Sleepbox nap pod hotel is between gates A6 and A14. There’s a nursing room near Gate A20, and free charging stations can be found throughout the Concourse.

**Concourse B:** Gates B38-B81. Features 13,000 square feet of retail space, and free charging stations at all gates. The FunWay children's play area and a nursing room are located near door B70, and there are smoking areas across from gate B37 and off gate B73.

**Concourse C:** Gates C1-C28. Free charging stations can be found throughout the Concourse. There is a nursing room near Gate C11 and a smoking area across from Gate C2.

**Concourse D:** Gates D1-D32. Amenities here include a nursing room and a pet relief area, both near Gate D1, a smoking area opposite Gate D30, and free charging stations throughout the Concourse.

**Z Gates:** Connected to the Main Terminal, this 20,800-square-foot mini concourse has only four gates, Gates Z6-Z10.

### Getting Between the Terminal and Concourses

![Image 1: Dulles airport.](https://going-cms-strapi.s3.amazonaws.com/64d12a2c4ecd7c4006df29eb_dulles1_3e795cd8ca.webp)

The 24-hour Aerotrain runs underground between the Terminal and Concourses A, B and C. If your gate is in Concourse D, take the Aerotrain to Concourse C and walk. Note that the Terminal Station for the Aerotrain is past security, and travel time between stations is less than two minutes.

A 1,000-foot passenger walkway connects the Terminal and Concourse B, featuring moving sidewalks in both directions.

Dulles also has 19 Mobile Lounges, elevated airport vehicles that date back to the1960s and run between the Main Terminal and Concourses A and D. Each of these vehicles can transport about 100 passengers directly to their aircraft without the need to walk on the airfield. They run every five minutes, and direct trips can take up to 15 minutes.

[![Image 2: CTA app download 1](https://going-cms-strapi.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/app_download_1_88de468c0b.webp)](https://app.going.com/DeR7/dl)

Flying In, Out, or Through the Dulles Airport 
----------------------------------------------

### Security and Customs

Dulles has three TSA Security Checkpoints: East, West, and TSA Precheck. All are accessed from the Departures - Ticketing/Check-In Level. Wait times average 10 ½ minutes, but on Fridays between 9-10 pm, they can be as long as 28 minutes. Checking the Dulles map can help locate the nearest checkpoint and save time.

![Image 3: map of Dulles security checkpoints.](https://going-cms-strapi.s3.amazonaws.com/64d12a3db81d479327f62e80_dulles2_c105962064.webp)

Security hours of operation are:

*   **East Security Checkpoint**: 3:45 am - 10:30 pm
*   **West Security Checkpoint**: 8 am - 12 pm & 1:30 pm - 7 pm
*   **TSA Precheck:** 4:30 am to 10 pm

### **Global Entry at IAD**

Global Entry kiosks are available in Customs for international arrivals.

### **CLEAR at IAD**

CLEAR kiosks are available at the lower-level East Security Checkpoint and at the entrance of the TSA Precheck on the Ticketing Level of the Terminal.

### **Mobile Passport at IAD**

Dulles enables you to use this [expedited security app](https://mobilepassport.us/) on your smartphone or tablet. Once you land at IAD, connect to wi-fi (or use cellular data), submit your trip data, and within a few seconds, you’ll receive a receipt with an encrypted barcode. Your receipt will be valid for 4 hours. You’ll then be able to skip the lines by following the Mobile Passport Control signs, showing your passport to the Customs officer, and scanning the barcode on the receipt.

### **Arrival Times**

*   International departures: at least 3.5 hours before your flight
*   Domestic departures: at least 2 hours before your flight

Metro delays and traffic congestion are common issues, so it’s _also_ advisable to allow extra travel time to the airport.

### IAD Wifi and Charging Stations

Free Wi-Fi access is available in the Terminal and all concourses. To connect, choose the "FlyDulles" network.

Free charging stations are located throughout each concourse in gate areas, in the Concourse B food court near Gate B73, and in the Terminal outside the International Arrivals doorway.

### Connecting Flights at IAD

The 24-hour AeroTrain connects the Main Terminal and the A, B and C concourses. The Terminal station is just past the security checkpoints. For landings or connections at Concourse D, Mobile Lounges are your best bet for transportation; these vehicles run every five minutes, and direct trips can take up to 15 minutes.

![Image 4: Dulles concourse map.](https://going-cms-strapi.s3.amazonaws.com/64d12a52179d2740c1880904_dulles3_30d31cbbe4.webp)

Passengers arriving at IAD on most international flights won’t ride the AeroTrain because they have to clear U.S. customs first. For international arrivals making a connection, there are Global Entry kiosks and a dedicated Mobile Passport lane.

**Minimum connection times at IAD:**

*   Domestic connection: 1 hour
*   Domestic to international: 2 hours
*   International to domestic: 2.5  hours

Getting to and from the Dulles Airport
--------------------------------------

### How to get from IAD to Washington, DC

**Metrorail (DC Metro subway)**

The Metro bus 5A, the Silver Line express bus, and the Fairfax Connector Route 983 ($2)—see more info below on these buses—connect the airport with [Wiehle-Reston East Metrorail Station](https://www.wmata.com/rider-guide/stations/wiehle-reston.cfm) (Silver Line) in 10 minutes. To plan your trip from IAD on the DC Metro, [click here](https://www.wmata.com/schedules/trip-planner/).

Metrorail hours

Monday-Thursday: 5 am - 12 am  
Friday: 5 am - 1 am  
Saturday: 7 am - 1 am  
Sunday: 7 am - 12 am

**Metrobus Route 5A**

This [bus](https://wmata.com/schedules/timetables/upload/5A_200823.pdf) runs every 30 minutes to/from Rosslyn, Virginia and L'Enfant Plaza in DC. Also, it includes a stop enroute at the Herndon-Monroe Park and Ride Garage. Buses are available at curb 2E on the Ground Transportation Level.

At the airport: Board buses on the second curb after exiting down the ramp from Baggage Claim. The trip takes 50-60 minutes. It operates from 5:50 am to 11:35 pm (from 6:35 am on the weekends).

At L'Enfant Plaza Metro Station: Wait for Metrobus 5A at Bus Stop "J". The bus stop is located on D Street between 7th and 6th Streets in front of the Constitution Center Building.

At Rosslyn Metro station: Wait for Metrobus 5A at Bus Stop "A." The bus stop is near the intersection of Moore and 19th streets. The fare is $7.50 for this express service, payable by SmarTrip or cash. When traveling from Dulles, prepare your payment as there are no SmarTrip card stations at the airport.

[**Fairfax Connector**](https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/connector/) **Bus Route 981 and Route 983**

Local bus with stops at the Smithsonian Udvar-Hazy Air & Space Museum. Route 983 serves the museum and operates only during museum hours. Route 981 operates outside of museum hours. Both routes serve locations in Reston, including the Wiehle-Reston East Metrorail Station ($2). Buses are available at curb 2E on the Ground Transportation Level.

Board buses on the second curb after exiting down the ramp from Baggage Claim. They depart between 5:54 am and 11:51 pm.

[**Silver Line Express**](https://www.flydulles.com/parking-transportation/silver-line-express-bus-metrorail-station)

This bus connects the airport with Wiehle-Reston East Metro Station between 6 am and 9:40 pm (Saturdays, Sundays and holidays from 7:45 am). Travel time is around 15 minutes and buses leave every 15-20 minutes. Free wi-fi on-board. There’s a luggage storage area on board.

Tickets cost $5 and can be purchased at the counter located by Arrivals door 4. Metrorail SmartTrip Cards may be purchased inside any Metrorail Station.

[**Virginia Breeze**](https://virginiabreeze.org/)

This intercity bus service connects Blacksburg, Virginia, with Union Station in DC. The daily route, the Valley Flyer, has a stop in Dulles airport Curb 2A (1:30 pm) and also includes several stops in the New River Valley, Shenandoah Valley and Northern Virginia. Ticket prices range from $15 to $50 (Arlington, VA $16, Union Station $19).

[**Megabus.com**](https://us.megabus.com/route-guides/dulles-washington-airport-iad-to-washington-bus)

Bus service connecting Charlottesville, Virginia with Dulles Airport and Union Station in DC. Buses are available at Curb 2A. The bus makes three trips a day between Dulles and Union Station, and the trip averages 45 minutes and $15-$19.

**Shuttle**

Meet your shuttle bus or van on the Ground Transportation level, at section 1D or 1E. Popular shuttles include [GO The Airport Shuttle](https://theairportshuttle.com/washington_dulles/) and [Super Shuttle](https://www.supershuttle.com/locations/washington-dca-iad/).

**Taxi**

Washington Flyer Taxicabs is IAD’s official, exclusive taxi company, with 24-hour service to and from the airport. From the terminal Arrivals Level – Baggage Claim, head down the ramp at Doors 2 or 6. A customer service representative is available 24-hours a day. No reservations are necessary for taxi service. Washington Flyer fares average $55 to Arlington, VA and $70 to Washington, DC.

_NOTE:_ If you want a non-Washington Flyer cab, you’ll have to make advance arrangements directly with that cab service for pickup at Dulles; non-Washington Flyer cabs aren’t allowed to solicit passengers on IAD property.

**Uber, Lyft and Via**

Pickup zone is on the ground level outside of Baggage Claim, accessible via Doors 2, 4 or 6. The canopy-covered zone features numbered pickup areas for convenience. Airport drop-offs for all rideshare vehicles are on the Departures Level. Fares to Arlington and Washington, DC range between $50 and $60.

Things to do at Dulles Airport
------------------------------

1.  **Check out** [**public art**](https://www.flydulles.com/about-airport/arts-program) by DMV-area artists, found throughout the airport. 
2.  **Enjoy live performances** by musicians, singers, and dancers throughout the year. November, for example, features a month-long classical music series. 
3.  **Shop ‘til you drop in Concourse B.** From clothing and makeup to luggage and accessories, chances are good you’ll find what you “need” here.  
4.  **Bliss out in one of the two Be Relax Spas in Concourse B.** Found at Gate B32 and Gate B64, these havens of calm offer facials, mani-pedis, and massage services.
5.  **Try a Virginia-made wine or beer.** Dulles is set in Northern Virginia, so why not try some local tipples while you’re here? Vino Volo has a few Virginia wines on offer (the state is the birthplace of American winemaking) and popular Virginia brewer Devil’s Backbone offers IPAs, stouts, ales, lagers, and more. 
6.  **Consider a** [**Priority Pass**](https://www.prioritypass.com/) **membership for lounge access**. Space permitting, you’ll have access to the Air France-KLM Lounge in Concourse A, and the Turkish Airways, British Airways, and Lufthansa Business lounges in Concourse B. You’ll also get $28 off your bill at Chef Geoff’s in Concourse C. Annual fees range from $99-$429, and can include entry fees of $32 at each lounge. 

Things to do with at Dulles Airport with kids
---------------------------------------------

Dulles isn’t the most kid-friendly of American airports, but these are a few things your kids won’t want to miss:

1.  **The FunWay play area in Concourse B** (see below for more details).
2.  [**Public art**](https://www.flydulles.com/about-airport/arts-program) by area artists, found throughout the airport. 
3.  **Planespotting.** The rear windows at Concourses C and D have the best views of the runways, and you can download the [Planespotting app](https://apps.apple.com/lc/app/planespotting/id1367589571) to help make a game of ID-ing aircraft as it takes off and lands. 
4.  **Tucking into burgers, hot dogs, and/or pizza.** Dulles may not be a gourmet destination, but cuisine-wise, it’s kid heaven. Your tots will be spoiled for choice with Smashburger, DC Dogs, & pizza and much more. 
5.  **Donuts!** There are four outposts of Dunkin’ Donuts to choose from: two in the Terminal, and two in Concourse D. Kill some time just by perusing the loooong donut menu.  
6.  **Books and magazines at Capitol City Ink**. These bookstores can be found in the Terminal and in Concourses A, C and D, and each has a grand selection of kid-friendly literature.

Dulles Airport car rental
-------------------------

The Washington, DC area is well served by public transportation, but because it includes large parts of Virginia and Maryland, distances can be long. Unless you’re staying exclusively in downtown DC—where parking tends to be expensive—having your own car is a good idea.

That said, rush hour traffic on DMV highways is legendary, so if possible, avoid leaving the airport area between 7-10 am and 4-7 pm. On weekends, holidays, and at night, airport area traffic isn’t generally an issue.

Parking at IAD Airport

This is the closest lot to the Terminal, just a few steps away. It has two access points to the Terminal via the underground pedestrian walkway. **Fees:** $6 per hour, $25 per day

These lots are at the airport, and you can either walk or take their free, 24/7 shuttle to/from the Terminal’s Curb 2F. Use Garage 2 if you are flying international, as it is the closest for most international flights. **Fees:** $6 per hour, $17 per day

Set near the airport, this lot offers a Economy Shuttle from Curb 2F that runs 24/7.

Ticketless Entry is available at IAD Garages and Economy Parking. At the entry to the parking location, insert your credit card (Visa, MasterCard or American Express), then insert the same credit card when you leave the facility. No ticket is required.

**[**Click HERE**](http://www.mwaa.com/dulles/2540.htm) for passenger information about AeroTrain**

The AeroTrain replaced most of the current Mobile Lounge system that were used to transport passengers between the Main Terminal and the Midfield Concourses. The train operates on an underground dual track system. The AeroTrain carries passengers between the Main Terminal and the A, B, and C-Gates. The stations are located at convenient points along the concourses to minimize walking distances to the airline gates. AeroTrain opened to passengers on January 26, 2010.

Click on the map below to view a full size image

[![Image 3: aerotrain map](http://www.mwaa.com/gallery/Dulles_Transist-Map_2010_sm.jpg)](http://www.mwaa.com/gallery/Dulles_Transist-Map_2010.jpg "picture opens in new window")

**Statistics about the AeroTrain:**

*   Total Number of vehicles: 29
*   Waiting Time Between Trains: Approximately 2 minutes in peak travel times
*   Maximum Speed: 42 miles per hour
*   Travel Time between Stations: 72 seconds

**Construction Details:**

*   Estimated Program Cost: $1.4 billion - entire project including tunnels and stations
*   Construction: Completed in 2009
*   Opening Date: January 26, 2010

The **Dulles International Airport Main Terminal** is located in [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Fairfax counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), United States. The original structure, 600 feet (180 m) long and 150 feet (46 m) wide, was designed by [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen") and completed in 1962 as the first terminal at [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport"). Annexes to the west and east were completed in 1996 as part of a renovation designed by [Skidmore, Owings & Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_%26_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings & Merrill") (SOM), bringing its total length to 1,240 feet (380 m). The terminal is operated by the [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority"), which operates Dulles Airport as a whole. The terminal's design is a [suspended structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspended_structure "Suspended structure") with roof panels of precast concrete suspended between cables which span the width of the building.

The Main Terminal's design includes parallel slanted [colonnades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade") on the terminal's north and south facades, interspersed with glass walls. The [landside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landside "Landside") facade to the north is taller than the [airside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airside "Airside") facade to the south; a concave roof supported by cables connects the two facades, descending toward the center. A concourse and [control tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_tower "Control tower") extend south toward the airport's [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_apron "Airport apron"). The interior was originally divided into two levels: an upper story for departing passengers and a lower story for arriving passengers. Saarinen's original design included [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge") that ferried passengers directly to planes, reducing the need for long walks or [taxiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxiing "Taxiing") while increasing the airport's operational flexibility. The modern terminal includes four [airline gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_/(airport/) "Gate (airport)") known as Z gates, where aircraft could unload passengers directly. In addition, two basements contain security screening facilities and an [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)") people-mover station.

The 1950 Washington Airport Act provided funding for Dulles Airport, land for which was acquired in January 1958. Saarinen was selected that May to design the terminal, construction of which began in early 1960. After several delays, the terminal was dedicated on November 17, 1962, along with the rest of the airport. Initially, Dulles Airport saw lower-than-expected usage, but increased patronage prompted the airport's original operator, the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA), to contemplate an expansion in the early 1970s.
