and the FAA awarded a contract to expand the baggage-handling facilities in late 1979.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-188) HOK's expansion was completed in 1980.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AJ-1980-11-189) By then, customs facilities had been moved to an adjacent temporary structure with four mobile-lounge bays.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AJ-1980-11-189)

The expansion came just as patronage at Dulles Airport dropped sharply, in part because of the inconvenience of accessing and using the airport.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-190)[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Battle_Creek_Enquirer_c578-191) To attract business, the FAA began allowing small planes to load or unload directly at the terminal itself.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Battle_Creek_Enquirer_c578-191) The FAA rejected plans to add more airline gates to the terminal, citing esthetic concerns and a lack of space.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-192) Instead, in 1983, the agency proposed a "midfield concourse" in the middle of the apron, from which passengers could load onto planes directly.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-193) The first midfield concourse was hastily built and could be accessed only by the mobile lounges.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-194)

### Master plan expansion

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Master plan expansion")\]

#### Mid- and late 1980s

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Mid- and late 1980s")\]

In the mid-1980s, as part of a master plan, a consultant recommended doubling the Main Terminal's size, constructing a people-mover to the midfield concourse, and expanding the terminal's airline gates.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-195) New vehicular ramps were proposed to alleviate traffic in front of the terminal.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987a-196) The plans also included new facilities for several airlines that used the Main Terminal,[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1985-197)[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Business_Review_1986-198) along with a separate terminal for international arrivals.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987a-196)[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990-199) The expansions came amid rapid growth in the airport's usage, which neared 4 million by 1984.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-200)[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1985-197) The master plan was approved by the NCPC in 1986,[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-201) at which point was expected to cost $420 million.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-202)[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987-203) In the meantime, a clinic, baggage claim areas, and stores in the terminal were added, while the international arrivals area was revamped.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Business_Review_1986-198)

The [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") (MWAA) took over Dulles Airport's operation in 1987 and assumed responsibility for the expansion program.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987-203)[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-204) [David Childs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Childs "David Childs") and Marilyn Taylor of [Skidmore, Owings & Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_%26_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings & Merrill") (SOM) were hired to design a master plan for the terminal, which was rapidly approaching its annual capacity of 13 million passengers.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) Passengers in the terminal frequently had to wait hours to get their luggage, and the [departure boards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departure_board "Departure board") could not display all the flights.[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_1989-205) Concessions and security equipment had been installed throughout the years, intruding on the original interior design.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-206) Security concerns had also required the mobile-lounge docks on the south facade to be closed; instead, passengers had to undergo X-ray screening, creating a [bottleneck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottleneck_/(production/) "Bottleneck (production)").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)

The MWAA banned smoking inside the terminal in 1988.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-207) The same year, to alleviate congestion at the Main Terminal, the MWAA began constructing the international arrivals terminal,[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-208) which was designed by SOM to the west of the original terminal.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31) The MWAA also developed a satellite facility with a baggage check and duty-free shop in [Downtown Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_/(Washington,_D.C./) "Downtown (Washington, D.C.)"), which opened in 1989, further relieving crowding.[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-209) At that point, the Main Terminal's expansion was scheduled to be completed by early 1994.[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_1989-205) In the meantime, the MWAA added temporary gates to the terminal, which consisted of [semi-trailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-trailer "Semi-trailer"); since these trailers were intended as temporary structures, they did not need to undergo a historic-preservation review.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38)

A baggage-claim area was added inside the terminal in 1990,[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990a-87) and a federal inspection area at the Main Terminal was enlarged as well.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-210) The International Arrivals Terminal opened in 1991, replacing the international-arrivals facilities in the Main Terminal,[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-211) though the new terminal quickly became overcrowded.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-212) The MWAA was also constructing permanent midfield concourses,[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-213) replacing the temporary annexes on the main building's southern facade.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) The Main Terminal's annexes were tentatively scheduled to be completed in 1993;[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990-199) the extensions would incorporate a similar curved roof to the original terminal, which would remain visible from the Dulles Access Road.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-214) Despite calls by [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") officials to halt or delay the proposed expansion,[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-215) the MWAA decided to proceed with the renovation, the cost of which had risen to $319 million.[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-216) The control tower's radome was replaced again in 1993.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54)

By 1993, workers had upgraded the airport's utilities to support the terminal's expansion, which was scheduled to be completed in 1996[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Fehr_1993-217) or 1997.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Moore_1992-218) This was planned to be followed in 1998 by the original terminal's interior.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Fehr_1993-217) By that time, Dulles had over 11 million annual passengers,[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Fehr_1993-217)[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Moore_1992-218)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Arch_p._40-30) and airport officials were considering replacing the once-novel mobile lounges with a people mover.[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-219) Work on the expansion began in October 1993,[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-220) though MWAA officials were already contemplating further upgrades before work started.[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-221) To fund the renovation, the MWAA added a [passenger facility charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passenger_facility_charge "Passenger facility charge") to every ticket,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38) and it issued [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_/(finance/) "Bond (finance)") to cover seven-tenths of the cost.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Potomac_News_1996-77)[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Danville_Register_and_Bee_1996-222) The Main Terminal was lengthened to 1,240 feet (380 m), slightly more than twice the original length,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cullerton_1996-39)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) and the vehicular ramps were also expanded.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cullerton_1996-39)[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-223) The columns and roofs of the original building were recreated in the annexes,[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62)[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-224) though the annexes' roof cables were prestressed using cranes rather than sandbags.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64) The framework for the eastern extension was finished by late 1995, with the western extension still underway.[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-225)

[United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") moved into the eastern annex on July 1, 1996,[\[218\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-226) and the annexes were dedicated on September 6 that year.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Potomac_News_1996-77) Afterward, the MWAA announced plans to renovate the original terminal's ceiling, which required [asbestos abatement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos_abatement "Asbestos abatement").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) The MWAA was also relocating the concessions to provide more space for queuing,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) and it finished replacing the vehicular ramps outside the terminal in 1997.[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-227) Additional midfield concourses opened in the late 1990s, relieving crowding at the Main Terminal, where queues had frequently doubled back on themselves.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Field_1999-16) At the time, there were proposals for an underground walkway (and, later, a people mover) leading to the midfield concourses.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-228) Development of the walkway was delayed after U.S. Senator [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") withheld congressional funds for the project, stemming from a dispute regarding flights at Washington National Airport.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-229)

[![Image 11: The AeroTrain station in the Main Terminal's second basement](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/2015-09-29_23_37_05_AeroTrain_station_at_the_main_terminal_of_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_Virginia.jpg/250px-2015-09-29_23_37_05_AeroTrain_station_at_the_main_terminal_of_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_Virginia.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2015-09-29_23_37_05_AeroTrain_station_at_the_main_terminal_of_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_Virginia.jpg)

The AeroTrain station in the second basement (2015)

By 2000, there were proposals to renovate the original terminal as part of a $3.4 billion renovation of Dulles Airport.[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-230)[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_2000-231) Work on the pedestrian tunnel to concourse B was underway,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Civil_Engineering_2000-45)[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-232) and several parking garages were being built nearby;[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Civil_Engineering_2000-45)[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-233) in addition, the terminal's control tower was proposed for replacement.[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_2000-231)[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-234) An underpass to the new parking garages was completed in 2004 for $81 million,[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cline_2022-93) and the tunnel to Concourse B also opened that year.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9)[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-235) A 600-foot-long (180 m) tunnel for baggage was developed concurrently,[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-236) and the Z gates opened in 2005.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-237) By the mid-2000s, the MWAA was constructing a security checkpoint,[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-238)[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Infanger_2007-239) along with a people mover (by then known as the AeroTrain) leading to the outlying concourses.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._52-55)[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Infanger_2007-239) This work was budgeted at $1.3 billion and involved constructing two basement levels below the existing facility, freeing up space on the original upper level.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-USA_Today_j755-86) The control tower was decommissioned in 2007 after a new control tower opened.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54)

The new security checkpoint in the first basement opened in September 2009, replacing all the checkpoints on the upper level; a checkpoint for frequent travelers was retained on the original lower level.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Yu_2009-88)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_2009-89) The AeroTrain station in the second basement opened in early 2010,[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-RTS2010-240) and the airport's overall expansion was completed the next year.[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Aratani_i530-241) Additionally, in 2012, checkpoints were added to the Main Terminal as part of the [TSA PreCheck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSA_PreCheck "TSA PreCheck") frequent-flyer program,[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-242) and the MWAA began displaying information on security-screening wait times.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-243) The Main Terminal gained direct mass-transit access in 2022 with the opening of Washington Metro's Dulles International Airport station,[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Aratani_i530-241) and an airport lounge sponsored by [Capital One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_One "Capital One") opened there the next year.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Clabaugh_2023-92)[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-244) The MWAA announced another master plan for Dulles Airport in 2025.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-245)[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roussey_2025-246) Renderings of this master plan indicate that a walkway might be built south to midfield concourses A and B.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roussey_2025-246) That December, the [administration of President Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_administration_of_Donald_Trump "Second administration of Donald Trump") solicited proposals for the airport's redevelopment, including potentially expanding or replacing the Main Terminal; although Trump praised the terminal's design at the time, he criticized the airport's overall layout.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-247)[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-248)

[![Image 12: The main terminal as viewed from the west](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg/250px-Washington_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg)

Saarinen had deemed the Dulles Main Terminal "the best thing I have done".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163)

When the terminal was being completed in early 1962, the architectural critic [Ada Louise Huxtable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Louise_Huxtable "Ada Louise Huxtable") described Saarinen as having successfully created "a symbolic entrance to the nation", saying that the design had a similar effect to an ancient Greek temple.[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-249) _[The Baltimore Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Baltimore_Sun "The Baltimore Sun")_ wrote that the terminal's design was "vaguely suggestive of some oriental shrine".[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962-73) Paul J. C. Friedlander, of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_, said the swooping roof and slanted glass facade created an effect of "grace and lightness".[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57) The commentator Walter McQuade wrote for _[Architectural Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architectural_Forum "Architectural Forum")_: "It is likely that the most majestic single statement of this integrated expressionism will be his design for Dulles Terminal."[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-250) Saarinen had deemed the Dulles Main Terminal "the best thing I have done";[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163) of the projects he had been working on when he died, he had been especially proud of the Dulles terminal and New York's [CBS Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Building "CBS Building").[\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-251) Saarinen's wife, the architectural critic [Aline B. Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aline_B._Saarinen "Aline B. Saarinen"), similarly believed the terminal would be her husband's "best work".[\[244\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-252)

Although the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") wrote that the completed terminal "was too modern for many tastes when it was built",[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Danville_Register_and_Bee_1996-222) the [_Architectural Record_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architectural_Record "Architectural Record") said the building "was almost instantly regarded as a Modern masterpiece".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31) When the terminal opened, _[Newsday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsday "Newsday")_ of New York described the building as "definitely a design of the future",[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163) and a reporter for the _Baltimore Sun_ said the structure "looks better the closer one gets to it",[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962a-29) _Architectural Forum_, in a 1963 article, wrote that the terminal "happily will never grow into an octopus", referring to the lack of jetways.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-253) The [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") wrote that the walls, interior lighting, and control tower combined to create "a dreamlike appearance" at night.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haughland_1962-2) The architect [Cesar Pelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Pelli "Cesar Pelli"), a former employee of Saarinen's, described the feeling of approaching the Dulles terminal as being similar to that of approaching a "great temple or a great cathedral in the countryside in France".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64)

Several commentators described the concave roof as creating a soaring effect,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[246\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-254) and they also likened the building to a plane.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McDowell_p888-171)[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howe_1963-255) The [_Bristol Herald Courier_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Herald_Courier "Bristol Herald Courier") said that "no building of such size ever seemed so likely to take flight",[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McDowell_p888-171) and a [_Sarasota Journal_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarasota_Journal "Sarasota Journal") writer praised the terminal's beauty, saying: "The trouble is, Mr. Saarinen forgot to put in the engines."[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howe_1963-255) [Wolf Von Eckardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Von_Eckardt "Wolf Von Eckardt") considered the Dulles terminal, along with [Boston City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_City_Hall "Boston City Hall"), as "the greatest \[building\] on the American scene in a decade or two".[\[248\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-256) Conversely, [Morris Lapidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Lapidus "Morris Lapidus") wrote for [_Architecture: The AIA Journal_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture:_The_AIA_Journal "Architecture: The AIA Journal") in 1964 that, although the building's exterior was "beautifully bold and daring", the interior lacked scale or embellishing details.[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-257)

Retrospectively, a commentator for the _[Reporter-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporter-Times "Reporter-Times")_ described early reactions as negative, saying that the local and state governments had only reluctantly accepted Saarinen's design.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-258) A _New York Times_ article, conversely, characterized the building as having been perceived "as a bold reflection of American aviation" from the outset.[\[251\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-259) In 1977, when the terminal's expansion was first being considered, a _Washington Post_ writer deemed the terminal Dulles Airport's "one great strength", saying it "looks far more capable of flight" than ordinary aircraft.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Morris_1977-184) Upon the terminal's 20th anniversary in 1982, _The New York Times_ wrote that it was "considered by many to be a landmark of 20th-century design".[\[252\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-260) _The Washington Post_ referred to the terminal in 1989 as "inspiring from afar and maddening from within" because of the overcrowding inside.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-261) A writer for [_The Wilson Quarterly_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilson_Quarterly "The Wilson Quarterly") wrote in 1995 that the Dulles Main Terminal and the [TWA Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TWA_Flight_Center "TWA Flight Center") demonstrated how Saarinen "push\[ed\] design beyond the confines of the Modern Movement".[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-262)

A writer for _The New York Times_ said in 2003 that the Dulles Airport Main Terminal, like Saarinen's nearly-contemporary [North Christian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Christian_Church "North Christian Church"), "immediately seizes even the casual onlooker's eye with its dramatic shape and carries it heavenward".[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-263) The next year, the writer Mark Gottdiener praised the exterior as a "dramatic, austere statement" but said that the interior, particularly the inefficiency of the mobile lounges, was inadequate.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Gottdiener_2001-112) A 2006 book about Saarinen's architecture said that his design "gave structure an expressive dimension".[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-264) Roger K. Lewis wrote in 2010 that the terminal had aged well over the years, not only because the interiors were so easily adaptable to different uses, but also because the terminal's design was simple yet memorable.[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-265) Over the years, the building's design has also evoked comparisons to birds.[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-266)

### Awards and architectural influence

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Awards and architectural influence")\]

The [Greater Washington Board of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Washington_Board_of_Trade "Greater Washington Board of Trade") gave the terminal building an award for its design in 1964,[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-267) and Saarinen's firm received an honor award from the [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects") (AIA) in 1966 for the terminal's design.[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-268)[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-269) A 1976 poll of American architects ranked it the country's third-best design, tied with [Fallingwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallingwater "Fallingwater"),[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-270) and one of the most impactful buildings constructed in the U.S. since the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ames_v927-35) The Dulles Main Terminal won the AIA's [Twenty-five Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-five_Year_Award "Twenty-five Year Award") in 1988.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) The [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") issued a stamp depicting the terminal in 1982 to honor Saarinen's designs,[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Tower_j689-271) and the terminal was also included in the 2013 [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBS "PBS") documentary and companion book _[10 Buildings that Changed America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_That_Changed_America "10 That Changed America")_.[\[264\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-272)

When the terminal was first expanded in the 1970s, there were calls for the Dulles Main Terminal to be added to the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") (NRHP).[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Huxtable_o904-182)[\[265\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-273) This would have made it one of the youngest-ever NRHP listings,[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181) as most NRHP sites cannot be listed until they are at least fifty years old.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ames_v927-35) The FAA opposed the NRHP designation, as it would have subjected any potential renovations to a lengthy approval process.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181) The terminal was deemed eligible for NRHP listing in 1978, on the merits of its design.[\[266\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-274) Ultimately, it was never added to the NRHP because of the FAA's concerns that such a designation would disrupt airport operations.[\[267\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-275)[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-276)

When the midfield terminals at Dulles Airport were developed, they were built of glass and metal to avoid drawing attention away from the Main Terminal's concrete structure.[\[268\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-277) The original terminal at [Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Taoyuan_International_Airport "Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport") in Taoyuan, Taiwan, was modeled after Dulles Airport's Main Terminal;[\[269\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-278)[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-279) the buildings were so visually similar that the [Taiwanese government once erroneously printed passports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_passport#Dulles_Airport_image_incident "Taiwan passport") depicting the Dulles Main Terminal.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-280) Other airport terminals drew comparison to the Dulles Main Terminal, including the former passenger terminal at [Montréal–Mirabel International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montr%C3%A9al%E2%80%93Mirabel_International_Airport "Montréal–Mirabel International Airport")[\[272\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-281) and Terminal 2 at [San Diego International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_International_Airport "San Diego International Airport").[\[273\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-282)[\[274\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-283)

5.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_ref-58)** These dimensions are given by several sources.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._4.8-46)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960b-56) Some sources have given different heights of 64 feet (20 m) for the taller columns,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14) or 45 feet (14 m) for the shorter columns.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57)
6.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_ref-76)** One source says that the main terminal originally spanned 362,442 square feet (33,672.0 m2).[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)
7.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_ref-104)** Sources disagree on whether the original lounges could fit 90[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1961-97) or 100 passengers.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McCaffrey_v490-103)
8.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_ref-110)** Sources disagree on whether the lounges reduced airline passengers' average walking distance to either 150 feet (46 m),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haughland_1962-2)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bennett_1964-108) 200 feet (61 m),[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Pillsbury_1978-102) or 300 feet (91 m).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1960-109) One newspaper said that passengers needed to walk just 22 steps from the main entrance to the ticket counter and another 48 steps to the lounges.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962-73)
9.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_ref-276)** Some sources describe the terminal as having been designated as a landmark.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Infanger_2007-239)

Eero Saarinen’s Revolutionary Design of the Dulles Airport
==========================================================

SHARE[](https://facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/eero-saarinens-revolutionary-design-dulles-airport/7853/)[](mailto:?subject=Eero%20Saarinen%27s%20Revolutionary%20Design%20of%20the%20Dulles%20Airport&body=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/eero-saarinens-revolutionary-design-dulles-airport/7853/)

In designing the Dulles International Airport, Eero Saarinen re-imagined a jet-age world, solving the problem of growing terminals by bringing the passenger to the plane with a “mobile lounge.”

* * *

Major funding for _American Masters — Eero Saarinen: The Architect Who Saw the Future_ is provided by the A. Alfred Taubman Foundation. Pelkonen](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/eero-saarinens-search-architecture/7768/)     [![Image 14: Eero Saarinen: The Architect Who Saw the Future -- Eero and Eliel Saarinen Compete for St. Louis ](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/files/2016/11/AM_Saarinen_Excerpt_5_Arch_COVE-512x288.jpg) CLIP: 1:44 Eero and Eliel Saarinen Compete for St. Louis Both Eliel and his son, Eero, competed to design a new monument in St. Louis, MO.](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/eero-eliel-saarinen-compete-st-louis-2/7766/)[![Image 15](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/files/2016/10/mezzanine_543-512x288.jpg) Eero Saarinen’s Gateway Arch Completed Today in 1965](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/blog/eero-saarinens-gateway-arch-completed-today-1965/)[![Image 16](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/files/2016/09/28_Gateway_Arch_textless-512x288.jpg) Eero Saarinen: The Architect Who Saw the Future](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/eero-saarinen-film/7507/)

*   [TRANSCRIPT](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/eero-saarinens-revolutionary-design-dulles-airport/7853/#section7853)

TRANSCRIPT

Sometimes the problem and the times are right for an entirely new functional approach to a problem. No one asked us to grapple with the problem of the jet age terminal beyond the question of pure architecture, but i believe the architect has to assume that kind of responsibility.

The essential element of Eero's approach to architecture was: What is the problem we're trying to solve? Many architects will brush that off and have a creative will to make a scribble and say 'do that.'

He wasn't that way at all.

In the case of Dulles his first thought wasn't, 'what is it going to look like,' or 'what is it going to be?' His first thought was, 'How do we solve the passengers walking for miles.'

The jets are getting bigger, passengers are going longer and longer distances to the plane so how do you solve that?

We became convinced that some new method of passenger handling had to be found.

The soundest system seemed to be one which brought the passenger to the plane rather than the plane to the passenger.

We arrived at the concept of the mobile lounge.

The acceptance of the mobile lounge concept allowed us to make the terminal a single compact building.

We started with abstract ideal shapes.

Gradually we arrived at the idea of the curved roof. It occurred to us that this could be a suspended roof. The Ingalls Rink give us courage to go to the hanging roof here. When he did the Yale hockey rink he had a spine and then he draped the cables and put wood on top of that. Here he's draping cables and he's putting concrete roof on the cables. You know, you scratch your head a little bit - so it sticks with you like, 'Oh yeah cool idea - but how does the roof stay up?'

Eero Saarinen – Model for Dulles International Airport Terminal Building
========================================================================

[Back to Collections](https://cranbrookartmuseum.org/browse-collections/)

![Image 4](blob:https://cranbrookartmuseum.org/b9a31d3949b1882a09ed2f8508d538f3)Photograph by R. H. Hensleigh and Tim Thayer.

Eero Saarinen (Designer)
------------------------

_Model for Dulles International Airport Terminal Building_, circa 1960

Born 1910, Kirkkonummi, Finland; Cranbrook Academy of Art, Instructor, 1939-1941; died 1961, Bloomfield Hills, Michigan

**Maker:** Eero Saannen and Associates, Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, with Jim Smith

Wood, masonite, plastic, gesso and paint  
18 ½ x 144 ¾ x 46 ½ inches  
Gift of Rice University, School of Architecture  
CAM 1983.15

When Eero Saarinen designed the passenger terminal for the gateway to the nation’s capital, he envisioned a building that expressed movement and the excitement of travel. Dulles International was the first commercial airport to be designed specifically for jet air travel. After completing extensive research into jet travel, Saarinen and his team developed a building that was meant to be practical, elegant and monumental. Two years after this model was constructed, the terminal opened for operation.

Angular concrete columns spaced forty feet apart on each side of the main concourse carry suspension cables that in turn support curved concrete roof panels. The columns are tapered and tipped outward to emphasize the dynamic structural system. The roof rises sixty-five feet above the passenger approach, and forty-five feet above the field. The passenger services are organized on two levels below the single roof plane. Mobile lounges carried passengers between the terminal and the jets, eliminating long walkways and the heavy cost of taxiing planes. Saarinen wrote, “I think this airport is the best thing I have done.”

Craig Hoernschemeyer  
from _Cranbrook Art Museum: 100 Treasures_ (Bloomfield Hills, MI: Cranbrook Art Museum, 2004)

Check the Dulles map before you move through the terminal. In peak hours, allow extra time at security and use the shortest exit route to the curb. If you’re traveling with a group, appoint one person to take the map and guide others to the correct exit. Within four terminals A, B, C, and D, a shared central spine keeps gates accessible. Within each terminal, signs and moving walkways keep passengers oriented; runways are visible from the departures concourse, helping you gauge distance. The blue signage will guide you to shops quickly. To stay on track, take the official map app or the printed directory. Check terminal and gate assignments for your airline; some Virgin routes may appear under airlinesvirgin in the system. If you have several bags, use curbside check to drop them near the right terminal. Walk times between gates are approximate; plan 5–15 minutes depending on congestion. For passengers with mobility needs, use the connector shuttles that run between concourses; they run every few minutes and reduce walking. The design keeps the main gates within reach of the central security zone, which helps with queue flow and reduces stress for travelers. For quiet moments, a prayer room is available near Terminal D. Food and shops line the shared corridor, with several quick bite options and full-service restaurants. For ground transport, lower fares are often available with rideshares or prebooked shuttles; drivers offer fixed-rate trips to DC-area destinations. Look for the blue signs to ground transportation, taxi stands, and the Dulles Toll Road exit. The airport’s space features art by artists and rotating displays to brighten long waits. Terminal Layout at Dulles: Identify concourses, gates, and the central hub on the map ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ![Image 1: Terminal Layout at Dulles: Identify concourses, gates, and the central hub on the map](https://blog.gettransfer.com/wp-content/images/dulles-airport-map-a-complete-guide-to-its-layout-terminals-and-naviga-9t9ow4yj.jpg) Begin with the official map, locate the central hub–the white square plaza at the center–and use it as your starting point. From this hub, pedestrian connections lead to all terminals and concourses, with clear arrows to each gate range. Have your barcode handy; entry to gates relies on a mobile or printed boarding pass scan. From the hub, follow signage to reach the three terminals and their designated concourses. Transfers between terminals use covered pedestrian routes or short shuttle rides, depending on your gate number. The plaza area houses amenities to simplify a traveler’s wait, including seating, restrooms, and nearby food options. * Concourse A – gates in the A range; easy walk from the hub, with a dunkin outlet nearby and several seating clusters along the corridor. Look for the designated signs that show the gate number sequence and the next connection to Terminal B or C. * Concourse B – gates in the B range; connected to the hub by a direct pedestrian path. You’ll find rental desks and the Regency lounge in this wing, making it convenient to set up prior to a flight. If you carry a lot of bags, the main transfer area is designed to minimize backtracking. * Concourse C – gates in the C range; features a compact shopping selection near the central corridor, including kiosks and a Dunkin outlet. The route to the central plaza stays highlighted on the map, with clear turns at each junction so you can meet any connecting flight without confusion. Practical tips for a smooth move between zones: average transfer times between concourses stay under 15 minutes on foot for most travelers, with a few longer corridors near the far ends. If you must switch quickly, buses operate between designated stops near the terminals and can reduce walking distance when you’re pressed for time. When in doubt, phone the information desk and ask for Melanie; she can confirm gate ranges, direct you to the exact pallet of amenities near a specific concourse, or point you toward the closest shell for a quick coffee break. If you’re planning a hotel stay, Hilton or Regency options provide shuttle access to the terminal complex, with pickup points shown on the official map. For a seamless process, scan your barcode at each gate, keep the number of your gate handy, and head to the plaza area to regroup before your next leg. Navigate Between Terminals and Concourse Bridges: Quick routes for smooth connections ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ![Image 2: Navigate Between Terminals and Concourse Bridges: Quick routes for smooth connections](https://blog.gettransfer.com/wp-content/images/dulles-airport-map-a-complete-guide-to-its-layout-terminals-and-naviga-pepvkx9a.jpg) Use the AeroTrain to link Terminal A, Terminal B, Terminal C, and the concourse bridges–it’s the fastest way to keep moving between gates, and the best option for smooth connections. Signs along the sidewalks clearly point to the next stop, and the logo on each carriage confirms you’re heading in the right direction. If you’re open to a quick stroll, you can shorten waits during peak times by using moving walkways in open sidewalks. Always plan for 5–10 minutes of buffer between flights. ### Fastest routes between terminals
RouteEstimated timeNotes
Terminal A arrivals → Concourse B4–6 minAeroTrain ride; exit at Concourse B; follow signs to Concourse Bridges; open, quick transfers
Concourse B → Concourse C3–5 minUse connected pedestrian bridges; watch for airline logos on signs
Concourse C → Concourse D5–7 minShort walkway or AeroTrain segment; good for busy days
Any two concourses (general transfer)6–9 minCombine AeroTrain with the shortest sidewalk route; plan ahead to avoid delays
### Signs, amenities, and practical tips for smooth connections Follow the signs and the airport logo to reach the correct concourse bridge. If you’re booked on a tight connection, compute a 10–15 minute buffer after you track arrivalsbaggage and collect your receipt at the claim area. Post-security paths keep you within the secure zone; using those routes helps you maintain momentum and still enjoy good amenities–food options, seating, charging stations, and restrooms. The Washington Dulles Airport Marriott is nearby; if you’re staying there, use the garage and rental counters for easy access, and you can be back in your gate area in minutes. Days with heavy crowds call for extra planning: start earlier, go with the flow, and avoid rushing. If you’re going to a flight, always check live flight boards for gate changes and use the fastest routes. This approach keeps you going, helps you arrive with less stress, and enhances your overall experience. Where to Check In, Find Baggage Claim, and Access Arrivals on the Airport Map ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- Begin at the terminal front and use the map to locate your airline’s Check In cluster. Check-in hours vary by carrier, and over the year there can be shifts; plan for two hours before domestic departures and three for international. Have your barcode ready to speed scanning, and consider online check-in to reduce on-site time. Travelers coming from Herndon or using metrobus can follow the routes on the map for a convenient approach to the front entrance. ### Check-In and Baggage Claim on the Map On the map, Check In zones are positioned near the front doors, with counters grouped by terminal (A, B, or C). After checking in, head toward security and then to baggage handling. For arrivalsbaggage, follow the lower-level signage to the carousel assigned to your flight; distances and wait times are updated yearly on the map. If you have checked bags, use the airline drop counters in Terminal B or C and attach your bag to the barcode. For a quick break after clearing security, use the loungelocation marker to locate the lounge, with quick caffeine options at Starbucks and Geoffs nearby. ### Arrivals Access and Ground Transportation Arrivals areas sit adjacent to baggage claim; when clearing, exiting through the front doors, then turn toward the transportation hub. The map lists transportation stops, including metrobus routes and rideshare zones, plus car rental desks. For a smooth pick-up, head to the loungelocation and grab a coffee at Starbucks or Geoffs before you continue. If you need help, use the request desk for directions to your next connection, whether that means Union Station, or a route toward Herndon. The map’s routes and distance indicators help you choose the fastest option, with updates on days of peak travel and yearly changes to layout and stops. Parking, Rental Cars, and Ground Transportation: Best routes and pickup zones ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- Take the free shuttle from the arrivals curb straight to the Rental Car Center; it goes 5–7 minutes and runs 24-hour. At Level 2, use the kiosks or desks to pull up your purchased reservation, scan the barcode, and grab your keys. Luggage carts are available curbside and in the terminals, so you can move bags without backtracking, and symon at the desk can guide you if you arrive late or during busy days. This route keeps you in access with most airlinesvirgin arrivals and avoids circling the terminals. The most efficient routes to pickup zones start at the Ground Transportation Center, where signs direct you to the Rental Car Center via a quick line that feels like a small train ride. From Terminal A or B, follow the open signage to the curb, hop the shuttle line, and you’ll arrive at the center in minutes. The center organizes pickups by company, with clear square markers and colored lines to direct you to your counter; most desks stay staffed long hours, and you can depart soon after you collect your vehicle. If you arrive with a Virgin flight, look for the airlinesvirgin signage to reach the dedicated pickup area without detours. When you return the car, follow the departures signs to the return lane, park in the designated bay, and scan your agreement at the gate kiosk. The open cabs and rooms for processing make the turnaround fast, and you’ll exit to the Ground Transportation Center near dining options like Potbelly if you want a bite before heading to the terminal. For open-access access to luggage or a museum stop on your route, use the main access roads and turn toward the terminal loop–track the level and line markers to stay on the fastest path back to departures or to the next flight. Please note that the open hours cover days of peak travel, so arrive with the correct documents and you’ll move from purchased reservation to on-the-road in minutes, always with clear access to the world of car brands and rental company options. Security, Lounges, and Passenger Services on the Map: Locations and tips ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Arrive early today and pick the security line that serves your gate to cut the duration between deplane and boarding. The layout on the map shows security entrances clustered by terminal, so turning toward the right door name helps you stay on track without backtracking through the district. ### Security checkpoints and access Use TSA PreCheck or CLEAR where available to speed up screening, and have your ID, boarding pass, and liquids ready for the 3-1-1 rule. These services apply across all terminals, so a smooth pass applies whether you fly in the day or at night. If you arrive during a peak period, follow the map’s signs to the connecting area and board shuttles between terminals to reach your gate without a long walk. For late departures, short lines are common after the last arrivals pass through, making schedule planning easier today. ### Lounges and passenger services on the map Lounges sit on the secure side of Terminals B and C, and access depends on your airline status, ticket class, or lounge membership. Look for starbucks locations in each district to grab a quick coffee before you board, especially during a late night layover. In the food courts you may find potbelly sandwiches and donuts for a light bite between flights. The map also marks shop options that carry wine and snacks, plus service desks that can confirm exact location and opening hours. If you need help, ask staff about the nearest door name marker and its location on the map to minimize confusion about where to go as you move through the layout. For travelers who arrive with a tight schedule, these services can save time and keep your day on track, whether you’re flying today or planning for a future year. Drive routes to the garages are clearly labeled, and shuttles run between parking structures and terminals to support quick transfers during your journey through america’s gateway airport. Practical FAQs for Dulles: Hours, Wi‑Fi, Lost and Found, and travel tips ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Plan ahead: verify terminal hours and the curb pickup location before you land, then log in to the free Wi‑Fi to map your route here. ### Hours, Wi‑Fi, curbside pickups, SmarTrip basics * Hours vary by terminal and day; security typically opens about 2 hours before first departure, with shops and restaurants opening around 5:00–6:00 am and late runs for international flights. * Free Wi‑Fi is available throughout the terminals; connect to the guest network, accept terms, and start your session to check gates and arrivals in real time. * Rideshare pickups occur at the designated curb; meet your driver on the proper line and confirm your name before you step into the vehicle. * SmarTrip is a convenient option for nearby rail access at the Silver Line station; use it to pay for trips into DC and back, keeping your card loaded for easy taps. * TSA PreCheck speeds security queues; have your licenseid or passport ready at the checkpoint; your Known Traveler Number can help, but it isn’t required for standard lines. * Hotels in the area include Hilton Dulles Airport and other properties in Herndon; starting your stay nearby can save time on travel days. ### Lost and Found, shops, and travel tips * Lost items: visit the Lost and Found desk in the terminal or ask an information agent for the correct location; provide a clear description and a contact method; a reference code may be issued for retrieval. * Found items: staff log them and you may retrieve them at the desk with valid ID; if you cant locate the item, request a supervisor at the information desk. * Shops and services cover various options across the grounds; use the airport map to find a shop that fits your need, whether a quick snack or a travel gift. * Wi‑Fi reliability can vary with crowd size; if you cant connect, switch networks or restart your device and try again. * Ground transportation: rideshare, taxi, and hotel shuttles offer practical options; plan your route to the curb or ground transportation area before you leave the terminal, and meet your driver in the designated area. * Nearby stays like Hilton and other hotels in Herndon provide easy access; discuss your preferred option in advance and plan a pickup for your departure day.

Gallery details

Site overview
-------------

In 1958, Eero Saarinen and Associates were chosen as the architects for a new airport to be built twenty six miles west of Washington D.C. Construction began that year, and Dulles International officially opened and was formally dedicated by President John F. Kennedy on November 17, 1962. Saarinen’s design was centered on how architecture could facilitate the travel experience of the passenger in the new age of jet travel. The design of the roof, with concrete panels supported by catenary cables, stands out as an important technical feature of the building and allows for an uninterrupted interior space to streamline the flow of passengers from the unloading area up to the mobile lounges and onto the plane. His modernistic creation reflected the connection of ground to sky, and Saarinen was also attempting to express “the movement and excitement of modern travel by air.”The airport received praise after its completion for its architecture and design, and in 1966, the Dulles International Airport Terminal Building received the Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects for its “vigorous, free and graceful movement which we associate with flight, while avoiding literal and obvious analogy.”

Designer(s)
===========

[![Image 7](https://docomomo-us.org/resource/mobile/medias/image/147sff25bj0k5ydj0.jpg)](https://www.docomomo-us.org/designer/eero-saarinen "Eero Saarinen")[Eero Saarinen ============= _Architect_ ----------- ### Nationality American, Finnish](https://www.docomomo-us.org/designer/eero-saarinen "Eero Saarinen")

Other designers
===============

Eero Saarinen and Associates of Hamden, Connecticut were chosen as the architect for the Main Terminal building. The firm of Ammann and Whitney of New York was selected as engineers for the airport.

[Related chapter =============== District of Columbia --------------------](https://www.docomomo-us.org/chapter/dc "District of Columbia")

Commission1958

Completion1962

Commission / Completion details1958-1962.

Original Brief
==============

In the middle of the twentieth century, plans for Washington Dulles International Airport grew out of the need for another airport facility in the Washington D.C. region as the Washington National Airport (Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport) was already outgrowing demand. The second Washington Airport Act of 1950 was passed by congress to provide for the construction of a new airport. A site was chosen 26 miles from Washington D.C., and the construction of Dulles Airport began on September 2, 1958.

Significant Alteration(s) with Date(s)
======================================

Construction began on September 2, 1958 and the building was completed by 1962. There have been many significant alterations to the airport since its construction. In 1980 a fifty foot corridor designed by Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum (HOK) was added to the length of the Main Terminal. In 1991 The International Arrivals Building was completed 300’ west of the Main Terminal designed by Skidmore Owings & Merrill (SOM). In 1996 the expansion of the Main Terminal from 600’ to 1,240’ was completed and designed by SOM. The expansion reflected the original design of Saarinen, who planned for an expansion during the original design to accommodate the growth of the facility. The International Arrivals building was connected to the Main Terminal due to the expansion on the west elevation. In 2005, the interior of the Main Terminal was renovated and ticket counters and baggage handling facilities were updated. An additional baggage basement was constructed under the ground level. Other additions to the overall complex include the construction of temporary Concourses C and D in 1985 and Concourses A and B in 1998-99 which were linked to the main terminal through the mobile lounges and an underground walkway.

Current Use
===========

Washington Dulles International Airport is used for both domestic and international air travel.

Current Condition
=================

The Main Terminal is in good condition.

General Description
===================

The Main Terminal and airport complex sits on 11,803 acres in Dulles, Virginia, and the Main Terminal and complex use approximately 5,000 acres. The Main Terminal is reached by an access road leading to a three-leveled oval roadway that runs parallel to the north elevation. The 1,240’ long building is composed of concrete columns 40’ apart along the north and south elevations supporting an upward curving concrete panel roof held together by catenary cables. The columns punctuate the roof and curve over the top of the structure on the north and south elevations. The spaces between column and roof are filled with glass panels curved into the building. The form of the building was designed by Saarinen to be centered between earth and sky, and as Saarinen stated to “both rise from the plan and hover over it.” The interior space of the main level is one large, open area designed by Saarinen to expedite flow of passengers from the roadway to the waiting planes and to connect the interior of the terminal to the exterior. The ground floor contains baggage circulation, and an additional basement also serves this function. A concrete control tower is situated south of the Main Terminal. Additional later concourses were added to the complex and run parallel to the Main Terminal along the south elevation and are linked to the Main Terminal by mobile lounges and an underground walkway.

Construction Period
===================

The building was constructed with reinforced concrete columns 40’ apart supporting an upward curving concrete panel roof of approximately 1792 precast concrete panels held together by catenary cables, which allowed for the uninterrupted interior space. Glass panels framed by metal surrounds create large open areas between the columns that slightly curve in towards the interior.

Original Physical Context
=========================

When the need for Dulles Airport arose in the mid twentieth century, the entire functionality of how an airport works and operates was studied by Eero Saarinen to design an efficient new airport specifically geared for jet airplanes. Saarinen focused on this aspect of the structure when planning the flow of passengers from the drop off outside of the Main Terminal, through the building, and onto the waiting airplanes. A significant feature of Saarinen’s design was the mobile lounge concept. The mobile lounges allowed for the Main Terminal to be a single independent mass without what Saarinen called extending structural “fingers.” The mobile lounges were a modernistic design to bring passengers directly to the plane and to shorten the walking distance. Saarinen also planned for the growth of the Main Terminal and the airport complex and incorporated future extensions into his design in order to keep pace with the expanding airport industry. The Main Terminal was a modern building signifying modern travel by the jet airplane.

Technical
=========

When planning and designing Washington Dulles International Airport, Eero Saarinen employed testing the functionality of other airport buildings and incorporated his findings into the design of the terminal. Teams were sent out to record information about existing airports such as walking distance, interchange problems, schedules, weather, and baggage handling to incorporate all aspects of air travel into his design. The design of the roof, with concrete panels supported by catenary cables, stands out as an important technical feature of the building and allows for an uninterrupted interior space to streamline the flow of passengers from the unloading area up to the mobile lounges and onto the plane. Saarinen was also taking into consideration the jet planes in his design, with the mobile lounge concept reducing reduced airport noise near the terminal.

Social
======

Eero Saarinen’s design of Dulles Airport was centered on how the architecture could facilitate the travel of the passenger in the new age of jet travel. His modernistic creation reflected the connection of ground to sky, and Saarinen was also attempting to express “the movement and excitement of modern travel by air.” Saarinen was making a statement against static Federal architecture by incorporating the concept of movement into his design. Saarinen also extended the role of architect by not only creating a functional and stylistic design for the Main Terminal but by providing a master plan which would take into consideration future expansion of the entire complex.

Cultural & Aesthetic
====================

The architectural design of the Main Terminal reflects flight and movement but does it successfully in a non-obvious way. The airport has been touted as a landmark of modern architecture due to its simplistic means of fulfilling the needs of an airport, and the fact that the airport serves a complex function is the beauty of its design. Saarinen took an intricate problem and made it simple, and his design for the Main Terminal stands out as a prominent building in the Modern Movement.

Historical
==========

In 1958 Eero Saarninen and Associates were chosen as the architects for a new airport to be built twenty six miles west of Washington D.C. Construction began that year, and Dulles International officially opened and was formally dedicated by President John F. Kennedy on November 17, 1962. Dulles Airport received praise after its completion for its architecture and design, and in 1966 the Dulles International Airport Terminal Building received the Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects for its “vigorous, free and graceful movement which we associate with flight, while avoiding literal and obvious analogy.” In 1978 the airport was determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places before it reached fifty years of age, but because of its architectural importance it was deemed eligible before this requirement was met. It has been heavily praised from the beginning as a monument to modern travel. Major additions to the airport began in the 1980s with the addition of a 50’ wide skylighted corridor added to the south elevation of the Main Terminal. In 1984, when the airport was renamed Washington Dulles International Airport, three proposals were considered to address airport efficiency problems. In 1985 two temporary structures, Concourses C and D were constructed away from the Main Terminal which expanded the complex. An International Arrivals building was completed in 1991 300’ from the terminal, but by 1996 the International Arrivals building became part of the Main Terminal when SOM’s expansion was completed and effectively joined the two buildings. Two more concourses were added in 1999, Concourses A and B, further expanding the entire airport complex. D2, a Dulles Development Program, was approved in 2000 to improve the efficiency and growth of the airport, which included a renovation of the interior of the Main Terminal in 2005 to maximize public space within and to update the technologies of the building.

![Image 2: AeroTrainLogo](http://www.mwaa.com/image/aerotrainlogo.gif)

The Main Terminal AeroTrain Station represents a major expansion on the airfield side of the Main Terminal. But since it was constructed about 60 feet below ground, views of the Main Terminal will remain unblocked. The station spans the entire length of the Main Terminal (about 1,600 feet) and has four distinct levels:

*   Departures (49,600 square feet)
*   Arrivals (49,600 square feet)
*   Security Mezzanine (121,700 square feet)
*   AeroTrain Platform (54,500 square feet)

[Moving passenger screening operations to the new Security Mezzanine](http://www.mwaa.com/dulles/flight_information_3/mezzanine) will alleviate congestion from the previous screening location on the Main Terminal ticketing level. The mezzanine is also directly accessible from other parts of the Airport including Baggage Claim and the parking facilities.

The AeroTrain platform is a "side-center-side" arrangement. Passengers heading to flights will be able to board the train from the center platform immediately after people arriving on the train step onto the side platforms.

Despite its underground location, the design of the station is very open and allows natural light to filter in. There is an extensive system of skylights at roof level, which is level with the ground outside. Trains entering and exiting the station will travel through glass enclosures.  Two elevators in the station will have the appearance of vertical glass tubes. The station and the [AeroTrain System](https://www.flydulles.com/travel-information/services-amenities/aerotrain-washington-dulles-international-airport) were completed in 2009 and opened on January 26, 2010.

**Statistics about the Main Terminal AeroTrain Station:**

*   Platform Level Dimensions: 440 feet long x 120 feet wide x 39 feet high
*   Waiting time between trains: Approximately 2 minutes

**Construction Information:**

*   Design Contractor: Skidmore, Owings and Merrill
*   Construction Contractor: Turner Construction Company

A Public Airport for the District of Columbia: The History of Washington Dulles International Airport
=====================================================================================================

Ray Clark
---------

### Advisor: Zachary Schrag, PhD, Department of History and Art History

#### Committee Members: Paula Petik, Kenneth Button

Nguyen Engineering Building, #1605  
March 23, 2017, 01:00 PM to 11:00 AM

Abstract:
---------

On November 17, 1962, President Kennedy, dedicated Dulles International Airport. Located on the border of Fairfax and Loudoun Counties, Dulles International was the world’s first airport built to accommodate jetliners. Despite this distinction, the airport languished for the next ten years. This dissertation examines the reasons behind the airport’s failure to attract passengers and what led to its eventual success. First planned in the years immediately following the second world war the region’s second commercial airport was to be completed by 1955. However, the initial location for the airport in Burke, VA proved unpopular, forcing the Civil Aeronautics Administration to halt construction until it found an alternative location. One difficulty in locating a site for the airport was the resistance on the part of the Civil Aeronautics Administration and its successor the Federal Aviation Agency to modify their plans to adapt to political and community demands. Dulles’ design incorporated several innovative features this agency considered necessary for all future airports and planned to use this new airport as the example for others to follow. This inflexibility was grounded in the high-modernist mindset of the government. This mindset was also present in the architect selected to design the terminal building, Eero Saarinen. Saarinen also sought to change how the traveling public used airport terminals by giving the passengers who used the buildings priority over the aircraft. The result was an airport 26 miles from the White House that had to compete with National Airport for passengers and saddled with a terminal building the airlines found impractical.

The eventual success of the airport came after three events in the mid-1980s. First, the growth of suburban Fairfax County, especially Northern Fairfax County, brought businesses and residents closer to Dulles than they were to National. Second, airline deregulation brought on hub-and-spoke route networks. Dulles’ size and configuration made it an ideal hub provided it abandoned Saarinen’s mobile lounges for conventional concourses. The third event was a new master plan for the airport that did just that when it proposed building a midfield concourse. A final obstacle to the airport’s success, the cumbersome funding process necessitated by being federally owned, was removed when Dulles and National Airports transferred from federal control to that of the Virginia chartered Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.
